item.title: Fusing Phase Map Servoing and MPC for High-Precision Robotic Tracking of Dynamic Objects
item.description:
The problem

Industrial robots often work stop-and-go: move to a fixed pose, take an image, then act. To work on parts that keep moving on a conveyor, the robot must instead close the loop on continuous visual feedback, which is visual servoing. Conventional visual features such as points, edges and contours struggle on the textureless or specular surfaces common in industry. Phase maps from fringe projection are an alternative: a projector casts sinusoidal fringes, and the recovered phase gives dense, subpixel geometric information without a 3D reconstruction step. Earlier phase-map servoing work, however, dealt with static or slowly varying scenes.

A moving target adds two difficulties. Sensing and image processing delays make the measured phase map lag behind the object’s actual state, and the lag grows with target speed. Model predictive control (MPC) is well suited to dynamic tracking because it plans over future states under constraints, but applied directly to the thousands of phase pixels in a map it becomes too expensive to solve at a high rate.

How it works

The framework keeps the dense phase map as the feedback signal but shrinks the control problem built from it, so that MPC can run at the camera rate, and adds an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to look ahead past the sensing delay.

  1. Phase map as the feature. The camera and projector are mounted on the robot’s end effector. The difference between the observed and the desired phase map is mapped to a 6-DoF end-effector velocity through an analytically derived phase interaction matrix L, one row per phase pixel.
  2. Gradient-guided sparsification. Pixels whose phase gradient falls below a threshold ε carry little information about motion, so their rows of L are removed. In all experiments ε is 0.15 times the largest gradient magnitude.
  3. PCA embedding. The remaining phase features are projected onto d = 8 principal components, so MPC works with an 8 × 6 interaction matrix instead of an m × 6 one. In scenes with enough phase gradient, the reduced matrix keeps rank 6 and all six motion directions stay controllable.
  4. Adaptive prediction horizon. The MPC horizon follows the phase change rate: it stays at Nmin = 3 when the phase changes slowly and grows smoothly, through a tanh function, towards Nmax = 10 as the target speeds up.
  5. EKF prediction as the MPC reference. An EKF estimates the target’s position and velocity, propagates them over the horizon and converts each predicted position into a predicted phase map. MPC tracks this sequence as its reference, compensating for latency, and applies only the first control input of each solution.

Results

MPC/QP solve time 6.8 → 1.9 ms (median, Table 4) and closed-loop latency 12.9 → 8.3 ms (median; 19.2 → 10.4 ms at the 95th percentile), baseline vs the proposed M6 configuration (Table 4).
Target moving at 0.1 m/s: 100 % tracking success vs 33 % for the baseline, with a final error of 0.05 ± 0.02 mm over 12 trials (Table 5).
At 0.05 m/s: final error 0.04 ± 0.01 mm vs 0.07 ± 0.02 mm and convergence in 290 ± 40 ms vs 420 ± 55 ms (Table 5).

The simulation, run in MATLAB, compares eight controllers: two baselines (A, which uses the full phase map and recomputes the interaction matrix at every step, and B, which adds warm start to A) and six variants that use one, two or all three of the reductions (M1–M6). M6, which combines PCA, the sparse interaction matrix and the adaptive horizon, converges within about 20 iterations and has the lowest RMS error and the lowest, most compact solve-time distribution. A sweep of the reduction settings supports ε = 0.15 and d = 8 as the balance point: they give a 1.9 ms solve time and 0.048 mm RMS error (Table 2), against 3.5 ms and 0.042 mm for a looser setting (ε = 0.05, d = 12) and 1.3 ms with 0.081 mm for a more aggressive one (ε = 0.30, d = 6) (Table 2). Camera exposure, phase computation and the EKF update cost the same with or without the reductions; the time saved comes from the MPC/QP step. The tests used a 640 × 480 camera at 120 Hz and a single CPU thread on an Intel Core i7-12700, with the qpOASES solver.

In the physical experiments, the projector–camera head rode on the robot arm and the object travelled on a conveyor. With a stationary object, the proposed controller reached the same accuracy as the original phase-map servo law, with errors around 0.3 mm, but converged in about 20 iterations instead of 30. The EKF matters most once the target moves fast: without it the phase error shows peaks approaching 0.2 rad, with it typical peaks stay below 0.1 rad.

The authors state that the reachable speed is limited by sensing throughput. With the 120 Hz camera and a control period of about 8.3 ms, tracking is stable up to about 0.12 m/s; above that, phase noise rises as phase-map generation cannot keep up, so results for faster targets are not reported. The current implementation tracks a single target under relatively controlled visual conditions; faster phase-map generation and multi-object tracking are left to future work.

item.title: An Improved Graph Attention Network for Semantic Segmentation of Industrial Point Clouds in Automotive Battery Sealing Nail Defect Detection
item.description:
The problem

Sealing nails plug the electrolyte injection holes of automotive batteries and are laser-welded in place. Welding can leave defects such as bursts, molten beads and pinholes that compromise the battery’s safety and durability. The metal surface is highly reflective and textureless, which makes 2D imaging unreliable: it needs frequent lighting re-tuning and suffers from high false-detection rates. Traditional inspection therefore combines 2D vision to locate a defect with 3D vision to measure it, a multi-stage workflow that is complex, less efficient and accumulates errors from one stage to the next.

A 3D point cloud gives direct access to the shape of the surface, but many state-of-the-art segmentation networks, such as Point Transformer and Swin3D, rely heavily on RGB-D or intensity input. That limits their robustness when only geometry is available, which is common on reflective industrial parts. The defects themselves are also hard to learn. Defects of the same type can take very different shapes, a scan of about 100,000 points contains only about 1,000 defect points, and near a defect boundary the point coordinates barely differ from those of the surrounding surface.

How it works

LGASS (Local Graph Attention for Semantic Segmentation) segments defects directly in the 3D point cloud, so localisation and measurement happen in a single stage. It uses geometry only: the network input is each point’s surface normal, and the point coordinates determine which points are neighbours. The network is a U-Net-style encoder–decoder built around two new modules, one for attention and one for pooling.

  1. Scan the weld. A 3D laser profiler (OPT-LPC20, blue 405 nm laser stripe) scans the sealing nail at a lateral resolution of about 0.05 mm. An improved RANSAC algorithm fits the reference planes of the nail and the battery cover, and a circular region around the nail’s centre isolates the weld region for inspection.
  2. Watch the normals. Nearly every defect region shows clear changes in height and surface normal. Near a defect boundary, two adjacent points can have almost the same coordinates but clearly different normals, so the difference in normals between neighbours is a key indicator of a defect.
  3. Local Graph Attention Filter (LGAF). Each point is linked to its k nearest neighbours. LGAF computes attention weights from the correlation between a point’s own feature and its feature differences to each neighbour, weighted by their spatial distance, and aggregates the neighbours’ features with these weights. A large normal difference produces a high attention weight, which focuses the network on defect boundaries.
  4. Spatial Attention Graph Pooling (SAG-Pooling). When the encoder downsamples, each point is scored by multiplying a learned spatial attention weight with its normal difference to a neighbour. Only the top-ranked points are kept, so points survive only if they are both spatially important and geometrically distinctive, such as those on defect edges.
  5. Label every point. The decoder uses graph-convolution blocks with positional encoding to upsample back to the full point set, with skip connections from the encoder. It assigns each point one of six classes: normal surface or one of the five defect types (burst, pit, warpage, molten bead, pinhole). A class-weighted loss gives the rarer defect classes more influence during training.

Results

mIoU 79.26% and overall accuracy 99.43% on the sealing-nail dataset (mean of five runs), ahead of PTv3 (75.13% mIoU) and OA-CNN (74.04%) (Table 4).
Pinhole IoU 65.23%, against at most 60.04% for the compared methods (Table 4).
+2.59 points mIoU from LGAF and SAG-Pooling together over a baseline with standard graph convolution and pooling (Table 5).
220.9 ms to process one sample on an RTX 4070 GPU (Table 6).

The authors built a new dataset for this work from real sealing nails on inspection lines, with naturally occurring defects: 271 normal and 658 defective samples covering five defect types (170 burst, 112 pit, 132 warpage, 102 molten bead and 142 pinhole; Table 1). Code and dataset are released online. LGASS was compared with GACNet, PointNet, PointNet++, Point Transformer (PTv1 and PTv3) and OA-CNN in this geometry-only setting. Over five runs with different random seeds its mIoU stayed between 78.97% and 79.61%, and it achieved the best IoU on four of the five defect classes: pit, molten bead, warpage and pinhole.

The ablations show where the gain comes from. Replacing graph convolution with LGAF adds 2.19 points of mIoU, SAG-Pooling alone adds 0.46, and the two together add 2.59 (Table 5). Normals are the better input: with normals only the network reaches 79.23% mIoU, against 76.94% with coordinates only and 78.31% with both (Table 7). The class-weighted loss raises IoU on the minority classes, by 2.3 points for pinholes and 2.13 for molten beads, and lifts mIoU from 78.73% to 79.26% (Table 8). Inference needs about 2.8 GB of GPU memory. The authors note that LGASS may struggle with highly concave geometry, such as recessed nails with overlapping defects, where a fixed k-nearest-neighbour graph limits long-range context, and that rare classes such as pinholes still have lower IoU than the others.

item.title: Automatic geometric calibration and unwarping of rotating line-scan imaging systems using elliptical distortion of circular patterns
item.description:
The problem

A line-scan camera captures one line at a time, and motion supplies the second image dimension. How the image is formed therefore depends on that motion, and calibration has to describe it. Most line-scan calibration methods assume the object moves past the sensor in a straight line. Many inspection systems instead rotate the object: cylindrical workpieces, rotary surface profiling, panoramic imaging of rotationally symmetric parts. Each scan line is then taken at a different angle, a sector-scan (polar) geometry that distorts both the 2D intensity image and the 3D height profile. Calibration methods for rotating scanners typically rely on known angular motion, mechanical measurements or rotary encoders, which add complexity to the system.

The distortion itself carries the missing information. Under rotational scanning, the circular holes of a calibration plate appear as ellipses, and how the ellipses’ centres and aspect ratios change across the image encodes the rotation geometry. Earlier work used circular targets and ellipse fitting, but usually treated the deformation of the ellipses as a side effect of projection or misalignment, not as a record of the scanning geometry.

How it works

The method treats the image as polar data. A pixel’s column gives its distance from the rotation centre, r = x − xc, and its row gives the rotation angle, θ = k(y − yc), where k is the angular sampling rate in radians per row. The rotation centre (xc, yc) and k are unknown. All three are estimated from the ellipses in an image of a simple circular-hole plate, without encoders, mechanical measurements or auxiliary sensors. One polar-to-Cartesian mapping then corrects the 2D image and the 3D height map.

  1. Scan. The sensor stays still while the plate turns on a rotary stage. Each scan line becomes one image row at a new angle, so rows record angle and columns record distance from the rotation centre.
  2. Circles become ellipses. Under this sector-scan mapping, each round hole appears as an ellipse whose shape depends on its position. A single ellipse may be perturbed by noise, partial occlusion or imperfect edges, but together the ellipses follow stable trends, and the method estimates the calibration parameters from these collective trends rather than from any single precise measurement.
  3. Fit an ellipse to every hole. Hole regions are located (manually or automatically), segmented with an adaptive threshold, and their edges are refined to subpixel accuracy along the image gradient. After outlier edge points are removed, each contour is fitted with a direct least-squares ellipse fit. The centre and the aspect ratio ρi = rx,i / ry,i are recorded; ellipses with large residuals or unreasonable aspect ratios are rejected.
  4. Regress to find the rotation centre and sampling rate. The aspect ratio varies approximately linearly with the ellipse’s horizontal centre position, ρ = a·cx + b, so the rotation centre is where the line crosses zero, xc = −b/a. Because a small error in the slope a shifts xc strongly, the line is fitted robustly: RANSAC first removes gross outliers, then an iterative residual-based least-squares refinement (ILS) drops measurements with large residuals and refits, typically converging in 2–3 iterations. A linear regression on the vertical positions of the ellipse centres gives the angular sampling rate k.
  5. Unwarp. Each pixel of the corrected image is mapped back to the raw image with the estimated xc, yc and k, and its value is found by bilinear interpolation. The ellipses become circles again. For 3D data, each height value becomes a point X = r cos θ, Y = r sin θ, with its height Z unchanged. The laser profiler produces the 2D intensity image and the 3D height map from the same measurements, so one transformation corrects both.

Results

Rotation centre xc = −516.76 px with R² = 0.998 for the aspect-ratio regression, and angular sampling rate k = 0.00402 rad/pixel with residual angular error below 0.12° across all calibration holes (Section 4.4).
Circularity error ε from 0.21 ± 0.08 before unwarping to 0.02 ± 0.01 after, where ε = |rx − ry| / rx is 0 for a perfect circle (Section 4.5).
Standard deviation of xc: 0.5 px with ILS, against 1.4 px with RANSAC and 3.8 px with ordinary least squares (Table 3).

All experiments ran on a real system: a single industrial laser triangulation profiler (LPF2-050, OPT Machine Vision, 405 nm blue laser, 3,200 points per scan line) mounted above a programmable precision rotary stage. The profiler stays still while the calibration target rotates at constant speed, and it records the 2D intensity image and the 3D height profile from the same measurements. Three circular-hole calibration plates of different materials, metallic and ceramic, with different hole layouts, gave consistent estimates of the rotation centre and angular sampling parameters. Ellipse fitting reached an average RMS algebraic fitting error of 0.42 pixels. Unwarping restored the circular holes in the 2D image, and the same transformation reduced residual geometric distortion and improved the spatial regularity of the reconstructed 3D surfaces.

The estimate becomes more stable as more ellipses are used. Over 50 random repeats, the standard deviation of xc fell from 2.1 px with 5 ellipses to 0.6 px with 10 and 0.3 px with 20, and automatic detection with ILS also reached 0.3 px (Table 1). Spreading the ellipses widely across the field of view matters more than adding more of them: the paper recommends about 8–30 well-distributed ellipses covering at least 30–50% of the field of view. The method also stayed stable under simulated partial occlusion, salt-and-pepper and speckle noise, and defocus blur (Fig. 10). When the scanned angle exceeds about 10°, the regression is stable, with R² > 0.99 in most experiments.

The authors also state the method’s limits. The model assumes the rotation axis is perpendicular to the image plane and that the scan line passes through the centre of the calibration disk; axis tilt, wobble or a lateral offset of the scan line would need extra parameters. Very small scanned angles make the ellipses nearly circular, so xc and k become hard to observe. Strong lens distortion should be corrected first, and a warped or non-planar plate can bias the ellipse centres. For 3D data, the correction addresses distortion from the scanning geometry only; it does not model laser-plane calibration or focal-length variation.

item.title: Deep diffusion model-based dual structured light for large-format complex surface imaging
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting structured light measures 3D shape with high accuracy by projecting sinusoidal fringes and reading their phase in a camera image. A single projector–camera unit, however, sees an object from only one angle. On large or complex surfaces, protrusions block the projected light or the camera’s view, leaving shadowed and blind regions without phase information, and the measurable area is limited. Measuring from several viewpoints, or turning the object on a turntable, fills the gaps but is slow and impossible for objects that cannot be moved.

Adding a second projector–camera head covers what the first cannot see, but only if the two heads can measure at the same time with overlapping views. When both projectors are on, each camera records the two fringe patterns superimposed in the overlap, an aliased pattern that leads to incorrect reconstruction. Earlier ways of separating such patterns rely on colour filters and special optical paths, extra hardware, orientation or colour multiplexing, or a strict order of projected patterns, and some give up simultaneous measurement altogether.

How it works

The system pairs two synchronised projector–camera heads with locally overlapping fields of view and runs them simultaneously. Instead of preventing the aliasing with hardware, it removes it in software: a conditional diffusion model learns to recover, from each aliased image, the clean fringe pattern of one projector. After that, each head works as a conventional structured-light unit, and the overlap is used to fuse the two results.

  1. Two synchronised heads. Two projectors and two cameras are connected by synchronous control lines, so both heads project and capture at the same time. Each head measures part of the surface, and their fields of view overlap locally.
  2. Aliasing as a sum. In the overlap a camera pixel integrates light from both projectors, so its intensity is the sum of the two projected patterns’ contributions, I(u) = I(u; l1) + I(u; l2) (background light is assumed not to affect the phase). The pattern of one head is therefore I(u; ln) = I(u) − I(u; l3−n), which the authors read as a denoising problem, with the other head’s pattern as the noise.
  3. Conditional diffusion recovers the clean fringe. A U-Net with self-attention is trained in a conditional denoising diffusion framework. Training pairs come from the system itself: one head on alone gives the clean pattern x0, both heads on give the aliased pattern y, which serves as the condition. At inference the model starts from Gaussian noise and denoises it step by step, guided by y, until it reaches the dealiased fringe.
  4. Phase and 3D per head. With clean fringes, the four-step phase-shifting algorithm gives the wrapped phase and multi-frequency heterodyne unwrapping the absolute phase. Triangulation with each head’s calibrated projector and camera parameters then turns it into a partial 3D point cloud.
  5. Fusion with ICP. The overlapping region provides corresponding points, and the iterative closest point (ICP) algorithm estimates the rotation and translation that merge the two partial point clouds into the complete surface.

Results

Fringe recovery: PSNR 45.80 dB, MSE 1.85, SSIM 0.98 against the non-aliased fringe pattern (Section 3.2, Fig. 7).
Phase: at most 0.05 rad difference from the phase of the non-aliased pattern along a test row (Fig. 8).
3D: RMS error 0.057 mm for the dealiased reconstruction against a reference from separate, non-aliased measurements (Fig. 9).
Reconstruction error within 8 µm along sampled depth profiles of a prism with prominent protrusions (Fig. 12).

The prototype uses two TJ20U2 projectors and two CMOS cameras with a resolution of 3072 × 2048. Fringe patterns with periods of 100, 110, 120 and 130, each in four phase steps of 0.5π and with varied initial phase, produced 4043 training and 1583 test samples of 512 × 512 pixels; the model was trained with T = 4000 diffusion steps for 800 epochs. Without dealiasing, fringe aliasing introduces significant errors in both heads’ point clouds and in the fused result; with the diffusion model, the object is reconstructed successfully. A derivative-based recovery method from earlier work makes the fringes noticeably denser with local intensity amplification, and its point cloud is noisy with pronounced layering. On a prism chosen to accentuate occlusion, fusion widened the reconstruction range and filled sparse areas that a single head leaves.

The authors define the scope of the evaluation as truly simultaneous dual-head measurement with a local overlap. Other aliasing-removal methods depend on specific hardware or projection schemes, such as colour or orientation multiplexing, optical-path separation or controlled projection sequences, and could not be run on this configuration without changing it. Results are therefore compared with non-aliased single-projector measurements as the reference and with conventional phase shifting applied directly to the aliased fringes as the baseline.

item.title: Depth-adaptive calibration of line-laser 3D measurement systems using rational polynomial mapping and depth-independent misalignment compensation
item.description:
The problem

A line-laser profiler measures a surface by triangulation. A camera watches the laser stripe on the object and converts each stripe pixel (u, v) into physical coordinates (X, Z) in the laser plane. A full 3D point cloud is then built by stitching many such profiles while a motion stage scans the part. Measurement accuracy is therefore set by calibration, and two different errors erode it across the working depth of field.

The first error is internal. Conventional calibration rests on a single-plane homography, a strictly linear pixel-to-physical mapping. In a real system, slight tilt of the lifting stage, local non-flatness of the target, radial and tangential lens distortion and stripe-centre extraction noise push the observations away from that ideal perspective, and a pure homography cannot represent the non-linear deviation. The second error is external. If the sensor is not aligned with the motion axis, the stitched cloud carries a systematic shear, and an orthogonal rectangle comes out as a parallelogram. Tuning intrinsics or distortion coefficients cannot remove this shear, and correcting each depth with its own parameters multiplies the parameter count. Existing pipelines usually address either the internal mapping or the external installation geometry, and their joint effect across the depth of field is seldom modelled.

How it works

The method handles the two errors in two separate stages. The internal stage is a one-off factory calibration that fixes the pixel-to-physical mapping inside each profile. The external stage is an on-site compensation that removes the installation shear from the stitched cloud. An automated, motion-triggered workflow runs both, so no manual multi-pose target placement is needed.

  1. Sample the full depth range. The camera and line laser are mounted on a precision Z-axis stage that moves through programmed positions. At each height the system captures a laser-on/laser-off image pair, which yields a clean stripe centreline. In the experiments, six depths Z1–Z6 are spaced 30 mm apart over a 150 mm range. Five are used for fitting, and Z3 is held out for testing.
  2. Fit one rational polynomial mapping. The model keeps the perspective (homography) backbone and adds a bivariate cubic residual in the height direction. Merged into one ratio, it maps (u, v) to X and to Z with a cubic numerator over a shared linear denominator, 22 coefficients in total. Cross-multiplying makes the problem linear, and the correspondences from all training depths form one overdetermined system, solved by least squares.
  3. Model the shear. The installation error is split into three rotations: roll α, pitch β and yaw γ. With a yaw angle γ, a scan step Δy pushes points sideways by Δx = Δy tan γ, so a rectangle turns into a parallelogram. In the tested push-broom setup, pitch rotates the laser plane about its own axial direction and causes no in-plane shear, so β is set to zero.
  4. Measure α and γ. A RANSAC line fit to a scan of the empty platform gives a reference line L. Roll comes from a standard height block of nominal height H and width W: α = arctan((H′ − H) / W), where H′ is the measured mean height of its upper face above L. Yaw comes from a checkerboard: requiring adjacent edges of a corrected cell to be perpendicular gives a quadratic equation in sin γ. It is solved for every interior 2 × 2 corner cell, and the median is used.
  5. Undo the rotation, once for all depths. Every point is mapped through the inverse rotation in Z–Y–X order, Rx(α) Ry(β) Rz(γ), which reduces to Rx(α) Rz(γ) with β = 0. The correction does not depend on depth, so angles estimated once at Z3 are reused across the whole volume.

Results

Mean absolute error 17.5% lower in X and 11.8% lower in Z than the HALCON baseline on the held-out depth Z3: 8.745 vs 10.600 µm and 3.820 vs 4.332 µm (Table 5).
Angle error of a 25° standard block, tilted installation: 0.7591° → 0.0387° depth-mean, a 94.90% reduction (Table 7).
Checkerboard orthogonality error, tilted installation: 10.007° → 0.309° depth-mean, a 96.92% reduction (Table 8).

All experiments use one commercial line-laser profiler (OPT-LPF2-006-01) on a programmable Z-stage and a push-broom rig. Ground truth comes from certified standards: a grid distortion target with a 49 × 49 dot array at 1 mm pitch, a metal checkerboard with 25 mm cells, a 25° standard angle block and a height block. For the internal stage, the HALCON baseline and the proposed mapping used the same image stack, the same stripe-centre extractor and the same train/test depth split. Besides the lower mean absolute errors, the proposed mapping improved repeatability by 33.8% in X and 70.0% in Z. The largest gain is in Z repeatability, the metric most sensitive to height-direction nonlinearity, which the cubic residual is designed to absorb. A sweep over the residual order supports the cubic choice: a quadratic residual underfits, and a quartic one reaches the lowest training error, but its held-out error rises to 12.155 µm in X and 5.130 µm in Z, against 8.745 and 3.820 µm for the cubic residual (Table 11).

For the external stage, the sensor was deliberately tilted (roll α ≈ 5°, yaw γ ≈ 10°) and measured at all six depths in three states: normal installation, tilted without compensation, and tilted with compensation, with 10 trials each. Compared with normal installation, the tilt raised the angle-block error by a factor of 18.84 and the orthogonality error by a factor of 31.87. With the angles frozen from Z3, compensation brought both back to the level of normal installation (0.96× and 0.98× of it). The per-depth reduction stayed within 94.69%–95.04% for the angle and 96.87%–96.97% for orthogonality, so one compensator handles every depth without retuning.

Both stages are needed. With the external compensator disabled, the mapping errors match the full pipeline, but the angle and orthogonality errors stay at their uncompensated levels. With HALCON’s mapping plus the external compensator, the geometric errors drop to 0.0506° and 0.519°, but stay above the full pipeline’s 0.0387° and 0.309°, and the mapping errors return to the baseline (Table 10). The compensator also kept working beyond the vendor’s nominal 5° mounting tolerance: at Z3, with roll swept up to 20° at a yaw of about 10°, the corrected angle error stayed within 0.037°–0.101° and the orthogonality error within 0.16°–0.59° (Table 9). The numerical part of a full calibration takes about 2.3 s, and the total of about 11 minutes is dominated by physical scanning (Table 12).

The authors scope these results to the single tested device and working-distance range. Validation on a second camera, additional standard angles and the repeatability of the estimated angles across independent re-mountings are left to future work.

item.title: Dynamic correlation network and structure-aware matching for robust point cloud registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that align two partially overlapping 3D scans of the same scene, for example LiDAR or RGB-D scans captured from different viewpoints. Learned methods describe each point by features aggregated from its neighbourhood and then match points across the scans. When the relative rotation between the scans is large, these features, and the correlations between them, can change with the orientation, and the matches become unstable.

The common remedy is to train with randomly rotated scans, but augmentation cannot cover the continuous space of 3D rotations, SO(3), so orientations not seen in training still degrade performance. Rotation-equivariant networks such as PARE-Net help, yet they still combine neighbouring features through a fixed MLP that applies the same correlation model to every neighbourhood. And even when two superpoints are correctly matched, the individual points inside them can still be paired wrongly.

How it works

The method follows the coarse-to-fine pattern: a backbone extracts coarse superpoints and dense point features, superpoints are matched first, and points are then matched only inside matched superpoint patches. It changes two parts of this pipeline. A Dynamic Correlation Network (DCN) inside the PAREConv-FPN backbone decides how to combine neighbouring features from rotation-invariant cues, and a Structure-Aware Point Matching (SAPM) module refines the point matches inside each patch.

  1. Rotated input. The two scans arrive at an arbitrary relative rotation; the network has to estimate the rigid transform between them even when that orientation was not seen during training.
  2. A rotation-invariant cue. For each point and its nearest neighbours, a vector-neuron encoder builds features from the relative offsets, the mean offset of the neighbourhood and their cross product. These features rotate with the scan; their magnitudes do not, so the magnitudes serve as a rotation-invariant descriptor.
  3. Dynamic kernels. A channel reallocation network turns that descriptor into softmax scores over a small bank of learnable kernels (four in the experiments), and each neighbour’s kernel is the score-weighted sum of the bank. Because the scores depend only on invariant quantities, kernel selection does not change with rotation, while the aggregated features remain rotation-equivariant.
  4. Context inside each patch. Each matched superpoint pair defines two local patches. SAPM refines every point’s descriptor with linear self-attention over its own patch, at a cost linear in the patch size; points that lie closer to a different superpoint are masked out.
  5. Consistent matches and the pose. A row-wise and a column-wise masked softmax over the patch similarity matrix are fused with per-point confidence scores, and mutual top-k entries become dense matches. Each patch yields a pose hypothesis by SVD, and a feature-based hypothesis proposer keeps the best one, without RANSAC.

Results

Registration recall 95.4 % on 3DMatch and 79.6 % on 3DLoMatch; the 3DLoMatch result is the highest of all methods compared (Table 3).
Transformation recall 82.3 % on 3DLoMatch and 82.7 % on rotated 3DLoMatch, where FCGF drops by 15.1 points (Table 4).
Rotation error 0.21° on KITTI, the lowest of the compared methods, with 4.8 cm translation error and 99.8 % recall (Table 2).

3DMatch and 3DLoMatch are indoor benchmarks with overlaps above 30 % and between 10 % and 30 %; KITTI consists of outdoor driving scans. On 3DMatch the method is close to the best RANSAC-based method, BUFFER-X (95.6 %), and slightly ahead of DFAT and PARE-Net (both 94.9 %); with RANSAC in place of its own estimator it still reaches 95.2 % and 79.3 %. When arbitrary rotations are applied to 3DLoMatch, methods that rely mainly on rotation augmentation, such as FCGF and Predator, lose transformation recall, whereas methods with rotation-invariant or equivariant designs, this one included, stay stable. On KITTI, CAST has a lower translation error (2.5 cm), while this method has the lowest rotation error. In the KITTI ablation, DCN and SAPM each reduce the errors on their own, and together they lower the rotation error from 0.239° to 0.211° and the translation error from 5.5 cm to 4.8 cm (Table 6). The model has 4.04 M parameters and takes 100.29 ms on an RTX 4090, faster than CAST (129.80 ms) and PARE-Net (122.80 ms) (Table 5).

The authors note two limitations: when the overlap is critically small, coarse superpoint matches can be wrong, and highly repetitive structures can produce ambiguous descriptors that mislead hypothesis selection.

item.title: Few-Shot 6D Object Pose Estimation via Decoupled Rotation and Translation with Viewpoint Encoding
item.description:
The problem

6D pose estimation recovers an object’s 3D rotation and 3D translation relative to the camera, a core step for robotic grasping, autonomous driving and augmented reality. Depth sensors are affected by noise, occlusion and cost, and struggle with reflective or transparent objects, which motivates methods that use a single RGB image. Monocular methods based on keypoints, templates or direct regression have made steady progress, but they rely heavily on large annotated real datasets, and the scarcity of real pose annotations limits further gains.

This work decouples rotation from translation. Rotation is learned from synthetic images alone, so only the translation part is trained on real images, and it does not have to learn rotation from them, which reduces the number of real samples needed.

How it works

An object detector first crops the object from the image. Rotation and translation are then estimated by two independent branches. The rotation branch factorises the full rotation R into an out-of-plane part Rγ (the object’s viewpoint) and an in-plane part Rθ (a rotation about the camera’s optical axis), R = RθRγ, and handles each with modules trained on synthetic images only. The translation branch builds on GDR-Net and is the only part trained on real images.

  1. Detect and crop. An object detector extracts a 128×128 region of interest (ROI) around the object from the RGB image; both branches work on this crop.
  2. Retrieve candidate viewpoints. A viewpoint encoder, trained on images rendered from ShapeNet, maps the ROI to a 64-dimensional vector that is sensitive to viewpoint but invariant to in-plane rotation. For the target object, 4,000 viewpoints are sampled uniformly on a sphere around its mesh and rendered to build a codebook; cosine similarity against the codebook gives the top-K candidate viewpoints.
  3. Regress the in-plane rotation. For each candidate, a regression head compares the ROI with the view rendered at that viewpoint and predicts the in-plane rotation, giving a complete 3D rotation hypothesis.
  4. Verify the orientation. A verification head scores how consistent each hypothesis is with the ROI, and the highest-scoring hypothesis is taken as the rotation estimate.
  5. Regress the translation. Following GDR-Net, a ResNet-34 predicts three 64×64 maps from the ROI (a dense 2D–3D correspondence map, a surface-region attention map and a visible-object mask), and a lightweight network regresses the scale-invariant translation from the correspondence and surface-region maps. This branch is trained with 600 real images per object.

Results

65.3 % ADD(-S) on LM-O, against 62.2 % for GDR-Net (Table 2).
65.9 % ADD(-S) and 92.4 % AUC of ADD-S on YCB-V, against 60.1 % and 91.6 % for GDR-Net (Table 4).
97.6 % ADD(-S) on LINEMOD with ground-truth ROIs, and 94.8 % with Fast R-CNN detections (Table 1).
Retrained with the same 600 real images, ZebraPose and CheckerPose reach 38.2 % and 40.5 % on LM-O (Table 3).

The evaluation uses LINEMOD (13 objects in cluttered scenes), LM-O (8 partly occluded objects, 1,214 test images) and YCB-V (21 objects, with severe occlusion and several symmetric objects). A pose counts as correct when its ADD(-S) error is below 10 % of the object’s diameter; for YCB-V the area under the ADD(-S) curve up to 10 cm is reported as well. The rotation network is trained on synthetic images only and the translation network on 600 real images per object; for YCB-V, physically based rendered images are also used in training.

On LM-O the method is ahead of the compared methods on most objects, with the largest gains over GDR-Net on Holepuncher (74.5 % against 60.1 %), Duck and Ape; GDR-Net remains slightly better on Can and Eggbox. On YCB-V it also leads in AUC of ADD(-S), 86.9 % against 84.4 % for GDR-Net. The few-shot comparison shows the largest gap: when ZebraPose and CheckerPose are retrained with the same 600 real images, their YCB-V ADD(-S) falls to 35.7 % and 37.8 %, against 65.9 % here (Table 5). The rotation modules were also evaluated on their own on LINEMOD: on real images with predicted ROIs, viewpoint retrieval is within 10° in over 70 % of cases, and in-plane rotation is within 10° in 74 % of cases with predicted viewpoints and ROIs and in over 90 % with ground-truth viewpoints (Figs. 5 and 6), so in-plane accuracy depends strongly on retrieval quality. The authors note that accuracy partly depends on the reliability of the object detector, and that generalisation to unseen object categories remains limited.

item.title: Robust Object 6D Pose Estimation Under High Dynamic Ambient Light
item.description:
The problem

Estimating an object’s 6D pose means recovering its 3D rotation and translation relative to the camera, here from a single RGB image. Gen6D is a model-free pose estimator: at test time it needs no high-quality object model, depth map or object mask, and works from reference images of the object instead. It runs in three stages: a detector finds the object and its size, a selector picks the most similar reference image for a rough rotation, and a refiner corrects the estimate.

Under high dynamic ambient light, with stark contrast between highlights and shadows, this pipeline breaks down. Reflections on the object’s surface change with the light, shadows alter its brightness and texture, and colours are distorted. The authors tested Gen6D in scenes where projected light sources make the object’s surface reflect unevenly, and its pose estimates were poor. The refiner often cannot repair this on its own, because it depends heavily on the rough estimates from the earlier stages, which the lighting has already affected.

How it works

The method keeps Gen6D’s detector–selector–refiner pipeline and changes the feature extractor that all three stages share. An efficient channel attention (ECA) module is embedded in the VGG backbone. The resulting VGG-ECA network weights informative feature channels up and noisy ones down, so the features are less disturbed by glare and shadow.

  1. Glare confuses the original model. On objects with metal parts, such as a knife or scissors, Gen6D often finds only the weakly reflective plastic handle and misses the highly reflective metal.
  2. Channel attention in the backbone. ECA modules are added after the VGG layers with 64, 128 and 256 filters. Each averages every channel to a single value, applies a 1D convolution across neighbouring channels (its kernel size is set adaptively from the number of channels), maps the result to weights between 0 and 1 with a sigmoid, and multiplies the channels by these weights. Unlike the SE module it builds on, ECA does not reduce the channel dimension first.
  3. Detector. VGG-ECA features of the reference images serve as convolution kernels on the query image’s features, at several predefined scales. The peak of the resulting heat map is the 2D projection of the object centre, and the scale map at that point gives the bounding-box size, from which the depth and the initial translation follow.
  4. Selector. The object region is compared with the reference images, and the most similar one gives the initial rotation.
  5. Refiner. A 3D CNN regresses the residual between the current pose and the true pose and updates the estimate.

Results

ADD-0.1d 51.48 vs 49.48 for Gen6D, averaged over seven GenMOP objects (Table 1).
Prj-5 91.94 vs 89.64, with the largest gain on the knife, 77.21 vs 69.73 (Table 1).
Inference time 0.5322 s vs 0.4965 s, 35.7 ms (7.19 %) more than the original VGG model (Table 2).

The model is trained on GenMOP, the official Gen6D dataset of 10 objects, and for testing the authors chose objects with highly reflective surfaces. ADD-0.1d counts poses whose average model-point distance from the ground truth is within 10 % of the object diameter; Prj-5 counts poses whose 2D projection error is within 5 pixels. On every one of the seven objects in Table 1, the improved model scores higher than Gen6D on both metrics.

Separately captured RGB images under high dynamic ambient light show the effect qualitatively. Where Gen6D boxes only the plastic handles of the knife and scissors, the improved model captures the whole object, and it also detects a transparent glass cup on which Gen6D fails. Across five light levels, from dark (L1) to bright (L5), Gen6D is much less accurate on the knife and scissors in both low (L1, L2) and high (L4, L5) light, while the improved model is more accurate, most visibly on the glass cup. The authors also report failures: strong light makes part of the knife blade appear black, so the improved model cannot detect the pose of those blade sections, and the metal scissors are still misaligned at L1 and L2. They name more objects and datasets, other attention mechanisms and tests in real industrial applications as future work.

item.title: Underwater structured-light 3D imaging method based on FP-DiffNet
item.description:
The problem

Fringe-projection profilometry measures shape by projecting sinusoidal fringes onto an object and reading the phase of the fringes the camera sees. Its methods and accuracy were established with air as the medium. Under water, several effects act at once. Absorption and scattering attenuate the signal with distance. Small-angle forward scattering from suspended particles blurs the fringes, large-angle backscattering adds background light and noise, and refraction at the water–air interface shifts the light paths. The fringes lose contrast and blur, so phase retrieval accumulates errors and the point cloud can lose regions or be distorted.

Restoration methods such as polarization or stereo imaging rely on prior modelling of the water’s optical parameters, while enhancement methods such as histogram equalization or colour correction can introduce colour bias and extra noise. Deep networks trained end-to-end avoid the priors but act as black boxes without explicit physical constraints, which can distort the restored fringes and bias high-precision phase retrieval.

How it works

FP-DiffNet is a fringe-restoration front end placed between acquisition and phase retrieval. It treats restoration as a conditional denoising diffusion process (DDPM): a U-Net learns to turn noise into a clean fringe image, guided by the degraded underwater image, and a simplified physical model of the degradation keeps the result consistent with underwater light transport. The restored fringes then go through the usual phase-shifting pipeline.

  1. Model the degradation. Following the Jaffe–McGlamery model, the light reaching the camera splits into direct transmission (attenuated with distance), forward scattering (a Gaussian blur of the image) and backscattering (background light and noise). Refraction at the water–air interface adds a depth-dependent shift of the rays.
  2. Train a conditional diffusion model. High-SNR fringe images captured in air are the targets, and fringe images of the same scenes captured in turbid water are the conditions. A clean image is noised towards Gaussian noise over T = 1000 steps, and a U-Net with self-attention learns to predict the injected noise from the noisy image, the step index and the underwater image. The loss combines SSIM, the noise-prediction error, an L1 sparsity term on the weights and a physics-consistency term.
  3. Restore by reverse diffusion. Sampling starts from pure Gaussian noise and removes noise one step at a time, with the underwater observation fed to the network at every step, until a clean fringe image remains.
  4. Correct with physics. A simplified degradation operator, a Gaussian blur for forward scattering plus a noise term for backscattering, links the estimate to the observation. Every k = 50 reverse steps, a gradient step with strength α = 0.01 reduces the residual between the observation and the simulated degradation of the estimate. Refraction is not in this operator; the U-Net learns it from the data.
  5. Retrieve phase and shape. The restored images have the form of standard N-step phase-shifting fringes, so phase retrieval runs unchanged: the arctangent formula gives the wrapped phase, unwrapping gives the absolute phase, and its difference from a reference plane is converted into 3D coordinates with the calibrated projector–camera geometry.

Results

Fringe restoration at the highest turbidity T4: PSNR 42.42 dB, SSIM 0.9750, MS-SSIM 0.9974 (Table 2).
Wrapped-phase MAE 0.0354 rad at T4, 0.0260 rad at T1 (Table 3).
3D reconstruction RMSE 0.0890 mm at T4, 0.0317 mm at T1 (Table 4).

The system pairs an industrial camera (1800 × 1600 pixels) with a digital projector (1280 × 1024 pixels) mounted about 0.6 m above an acrylic tank, using a three-frequency four-step phase-shifting scheme. Turbidity was raised by adding 4, 5, 6 and 7 mL of milk to 13 L of clear water, giving four levels T1–T4. The dataset covers five objects in random poses, split 4:1 into 7200 training and 1800 test images, and all reported results are on the test set. Errors are measured against ground-truth fringe images, phases and reconstructions. From T1 to T4, PSNR falls only from 43.02 to 42.42 dB, and wrapped-phase cosine similarity stays between 0.9951 and 0.9962. The remaining phase errors concentrate at object boundaries, shadows and phase discontinuities. Restoring one 512 × 512 fringe image takes about 430 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090.

The authors state the limits. T4 is the most turbid level tested; beyond it they expect restoration to fail once direct transmission falls below the noise floor and the fringe information is lost. The framework applies to sinusoidal phase-shifting patterns, and other structured-light configurations or underwater conditions may need fine-tuning with configuration-specific data.

item.title: Deep transformer-enhanced dynamic structured light for three-dimensional moving object imaging
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) projects a sequence of sinusoidal fringe patterns, each shifted by a known amount, and recovers the 3D shape of a surface from the phase of the captured images. It is robust to ambient light and to changes in surface reflectivity, but it needs at least three images, and the object must stay still while they are taken. If the object moves, each surface point is lit by different projector pixels and seen by different camera pixels in each frame, so the phase steps between frames are no longer the intended ones. The result is ripples, phase-unwrapping errors or a failed reconstruction.

Faster projectors and cameras reduce the problem but raise hardware cost, and the effect of motion still remains. Most error-estimation methods handle motion only along the depth direction and do not address the pixel mismatch caused by motion in other directions. Tracking-based compensation models such as Lu’s work well within the X–Y plane but handle Z-direction motion poorly, and methods that estimate a single global translation miss local, pixel-level motion differences. When an object moves in an arbitrary direction, every surface point has its own displacement and therefore its own phase error.

How it works

The method keeps standard four-step phase shifting and adds two things: a learned tracker that finds where each pixel of one fringe image went in the next ones, and a pixel-wise model of the phase error that remains after that tracking. Both run inside a short sliding window of five frames.

  1. Model the motion-induced phase error. The projector cycles four-step fringes (π/2 apart) while the camera captures the moving object. The motion of each surface point is split into an in-plane displacement, which moves the point to another pixel (Δu, Δv), and a displacement along Z, which adds a phase error. The total phase error is the sum of the two.
  2. Track pixels with a transformer. The image sequence is split into windows of five frames, and the middle frame is the key frame. A COTR (COrrespondence TRansformer) network, initialised with its original pre-trained weights and fine-tuned on fringe images, matches query pixels in the key frame to the other four frames. A shared CNN backbone extracts features from both images, a transformer encoder–decoder relates them, and an MLP head predicts each match.
  3. Align the frames and solve for the Z error. The matches define a pixel-wise mapping that aligns all five frames so the same surface point is followed through the window. Within the short window, the Z-direction velocity is treated as constant, so the Z part of the phase error is (n − 3)ε in frame n. Three intensity combinations of the five frames give three equations in the object phase Φ and ε. For small ε they reduce to a linear equation K1ε + K0 = 0, which is solved at every pixel, and the corrected phase Φ follows.
  4. Unwrap and reconstruct. The corrected wrapped phase is unwrapped with a three-frequency phase-shifting algorithm, using two sets of lower-frequency fringes projected alternately with the high-frequency ones, and converted into 3D shape with the calibrated camera–projector model.
  5. Slide the window. The window moves on by one frame, so each newly acquired image, together with the four before it, gives a new 3D shape of the object.

Results

RMSE 0.072 mm on a moving ceramic plate, against 1.401 mm for standard PSP and 1.352–2.028 mm for Guo’s, Lu’s and Wang’s methods (Section 3.2, Fig. 6).
RMSE 0.096 mm on a moving “Aphrodite” statue, against 1.129 mm for PSP (Section 3.3, Fig. 8).
Fringe-image matching error (AEPE) 0.47–0.83 px for the fine-tuned COTR, against 12.32–21.06 px for optical flow on five unseen objects (Table 1).
3D reconstruction RMSE 0.092 mm with COTR as the tracker, against 0.157, 0.181 and 0.490 mm with fine-tuned FlowFormer, GMFlow and RAFT in a combined-motion experiment (Table 2).

The system uses a high-speed camera at 512 × 512 pixels and 30 fps and a DLP projector. To fine-tune COTR, the authors captured 45 dynamic scenes of sculptures, toys and industrial parts on a sandbox, with 60 motions each, giving 2,700 pairs of pre- and post-motion fringe images (2,400 for training, 300 for validation). Ground-truth matches came from an extra blank image projected at each pose, on which a robust local optical flow method computed dense displacements. Training converged after about 1,400 epochs and took about 42 hours.

The ceramic plate was moved by a translation stage at 40° to the camera’s optical axis in 1 mm steps, with a 12-step phase-shifting measurement as ground truth. Standard PSP shows clear ripple distortion. Guo’s method smooths part of it, Lu’s method compensates only motion in the X–Y plane, and Wang’s method simplifies the phase-shift error, which leads to even larger errors. With steps of ±1, ±2 and ±3 mm, the RMS error of the proposed method stays below 0.1 mm (Fig. 6(f)). On the statue, PSP shows stripe artifacts and discontinuities along the edges, Guo’s method still has large errors at the edges, and Lu’s method leaves periodic ripples because Z-direction motion is not compensated; the proposed method recovers the contour more accurately.

The method was also tested on a static statue next to a rotating one, on a rotating fan model with a smooth, weakly textured surface, on a statue on a continuously rotating platform, and on objects that translate and rotate at the same time. Under combined translation and rotation, the rotation adds phase deviations of up to about 1 rad in the outer regions, and the method still keeps most surface areas accurate. The authors note its limits: when the translation along Z is too large, phase-error estimation can still fail (marked regions in Fig. 12); the authors suggest increasing the projection rate or combining the framework with geometry-constraint-based or Gray-code-based unwrapping. Because the estimate relies on a five-frame window, the method works reliably for small inter-frame motion; standard frame rates suffice for slow to moderate motion, while fast objects need high-frame-rate cameras and projectors.

item.title: Calibration Method of Fringe Projection Based on High-Order Polynomial
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) measures 3D shape by projecting sinusoidal fringes onto an object, recovering the phase of the deformed fringes in the camera image, and converting pixel coordinates and phase into 3D coordinates. That conversion is set by system calibration, and the traditional approaches are laborious. Phase-to-height mapping needs a large, precise calibration target and a precision translation stage, and its parameters depend on how accurately both are made and moved. Stereo-vision calibration takes the target coordinates and their image coordinates in both the camera and the projector, and solves for the parameters by nonlinear optimisation, which is slow, and its accuracy depends on the image coordinates in both the camera and the projector.

A polynomial calibration model avoids the projector model and the translation stage: it directly fits the 3D world coordinates as a polynomial in the pixel coordinates (u, v) and the absolute phase ϕ. Higher orders describe this relationship more accurately, but the number of coefficients grows quickly, and fitting them by least squares becomes slow and unstable once the order exceeds 3. An earlier simplification removes redundant terms by principal component analysis, which speeds the fit up but lowers reconstruction accuracy.

How it works

The method keeps a high-order polynomial calibration model, which needs no projector model and no translation stage, and replaces least-squares fitting with a sparse greedy randomized Kaczmarz (SGRK) solver. SGRK combines the efficient iterations of the randomized sparse Kaczmarz method with the selection strategy of greedy algorithms: each step works on one well-chosen equation instead of the whole system.

  1. Collect calibration points. Fringes are projected onto a circle-grid board placed in several poses. The circle centres are the feature points: each gives its pixel coordinates (u, v), its absolute phase ϕ from three-frequency four-step phase shifting, and its world coordinates from Zhang’s calibration method.
  2. Set up the polynomial model. Each world coordinate X, Y and Z is written as an n-th order polynomial in u, v and ϕ, so calibration becomes a linear system W = Ax. The model has 60 coefficients at order 3, 105 at order 4 and 168 at order 5; the paper uses order 4 as its standard model, balancing accuracy and computing time.
  3. Choose an equation greedily. In each iteration SGRK computes the residual of every equation, keeps the rows whose residual passes a threshold, and draws one of them with probability proportional to its squared residual. Equations with large errors are therefore updated first, which speeds up convergence.
  4. Update and sparsify. The chosen row updates the coefficients by a weighted Kaczmarz projection, and a soft-threshold operation then sets small coefficients to zero, so the solution stays sparse.
  5. Iterate, then reconstruct. The loop runs until the relative error of the coefficients falls below 10⁻⁶. To measure an object, the pixel coordinates and absolute phase of each point are put into the fitted polynomial to give its 3D coordinates.

Results

Standard ceramic sphere (25.0001 mm), 4th-order model: diameter deviation 0.0232 mm in 1.63 s with SGRK, against 0.0727 mm in 3.96 s with least squares (Table 2).
Standard step block, 4th-order model: average errors of 0.004 and −0.003 mm on the two step heights in 1.78 s, against 0.009 and 0.006 mm in 4.32 s with least squares (Table 1).
Ceramic doll: RMSE 0.0729 mm with SGRK versus 0.9250 mm with least squares, measured against a Mech-Eye Pro S Enhanced scan (Sec. 3, Fig. 9).

The system uses a DLP LightCrafter 4500 projector (912 × 1140 pixels), a CCD camera (1280 × 1024 pixels) and a 300 mm × 300 mm circle board with 30 mm between circle centres. Each method was compared on the full 4th-order model and on the PCA-simplified 4th-order model. SGRK was faster and more accurate in both cases: on the sphere the simplified model gave 0.0449 mm in 1.17 s with SGRK against 0.0932 mm in 3.17 s with least squares, and the simplified models were less accurate than the full one for both solvers (Table 2). The step block was measured three times after each calibration to check repeatability (Table 1).

The advantage holds at other orders too (Table 3). At order 3, SGRK gave a sphere diameter deviation of 0.0549 mm in 1.02 s against 0.1470 mm in 3.04 s for least squares; at order 5, 0.0177 mm in 2.31 s against 0.0400 mm in 6.15 s. The 5th-order model is more accurate than the 4th, but its 168 coefficients make the computation markedly longer, and both are more accurate than the 3rd-order model.

item.title: DeSC: Learning Deep Semantic Descriptor for NeRF Registration
item.description:
The problem

A Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) stores a scene inside a neural network. Large scenes are often split into several NeRFs, and images captured without reliable global camera poses produce NeRFs that each live in their own coordinate frame. To combine them, one has to estimate the rigid rotation and translation between two independently trained NeRFs: NeRF registration.

Existing methods rely on either geometry or rendered colour. DReg-NeRF samples a point cloud from each NeRF and regresses correspondences, but these point clouds are noisy and contain artifacts from inaccurate density estimates, especially when a NeRF is under-trained. VF-NeRF optimises with a photometric loss, which makes it vulnerable to textureless and highly symmetric cases. Both ignore the view-independent embedding that a NeRF computes internally for every 3D point, which carries both geometry and appearance. Using it directly is not straightforward either: the two NeRFs are trained separately, so their embedding spaces do not match.

How it works

DeSC treats each NeRF as a source of point features, not only of geometry. It samples a point cloud from each NeRF, extracts geometric features with a KPConv backbone, and adds a Deep Semantic Aggregation Module (DSAM) that turns the NeRF’s own embeddings into descriptors that agree across the two NeRFs. A Transformer and a coarse-to-fine matcher then find correspondences, and the pose is solved by SVD.

  1. Sample each NeRF. DeSC takes the centres of the non-empty voxels in each NeRF’s occupancy grid and keeps those whose density exceeds a threshold σt. KP-FCNN downsamples this point cloud hierarchically and extracts multi-level geometric features.
  2. Query embeddings around each coarse point. For every coarse point, a patch is formed from its k nearest dense points within a radius τ. Each patch point queries the NeRF for its view-independent embedding, which is enriched with the point’s colour and density through a sinusoidal encoding, so that the features carry photometric information shared by both NeRFs.
  3. Aggregate with a texture-aware graph convolution. A graph convolution runs over each patch. Its edge weights emphasise points that are close to each other but have contrasting features, capturing local high-frequency texture. The output is fused with the geometric features to give the deep semantic descriptor.
  4. Add context and match. Geometric self-attention and cross-attention let each point cloud gather context from itself and from the other. Coarse correspondences are selected from the resulting features and refined on dense points with an optimal transport layer.
  5. Solve the pose. Outliers are removed, and SVD gives the rotation and translation that align the two NeRFs. During training, a density-aware photometric consistency loss also asks matched patches to have similar density-weighted colour.

Results

Registration recall 97.7 % on Objaverse, against 92.1 % for VF-NeRF and 94.5 % for SIRA-PCR, with a rotation error of 2.57° (Table I).
90.6 %, 91.0 % and 88.1 % registration recall at 30 % overlap on DTU, LLFF and Mip-NeRF360, against 86.6 %, 88.5 % and 84.8 % for VF-NeRF (Tables III–V).
Removing all proposed modules lowers Objaverse recall to 93.2 % and raises the rotation error to 9.19° (Table VI).

The object-level benchmark is built from Objaverse: for each object, 120 rendered images are split into two blocks, each block is given a random transformation, and a separate NeRF is trained on each; 44 objects unseen during training are used for testing. Registration recall counts the pairs whose estimated transformation has an RMSE below 0.2 m. DeSC is compared with the NeRF registration methods DReg-NeRF and VF-NeRF, and with eight point cloud registration methods run on points sampled from the NeRFs. With uniform noise of 10 % of the scene size added, its recall is still 95.74 % (Table II).

On the real-scene datasets DTU, LLFF and Mip-NeRF360, each scene is split into image subsets with 30 %, 50 % and 80 % overlap. DeSC has the highest registration recall in all nine settings, and the margin is largest at 30 % overlap, although VF-NeRF reaches a slightly lower rotation error in some settings. In the ablation, adding the deep semantic aggregation, the photometric encoding, the texture-aware edge weights and the photometric consistency loss in turn raises Objaverse recall step by step: 93.2 %, 93.9 %, 95.1 %, 96.9 % and 97.7 %.

The authors state two limitations. DeSC relies on NeRF’s implicit embeddings, so it does not apply directly to explicit representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting, voxel grids or hash-based methods. Objects that are highly symmetric in both shape and texture, such as a traffic cone, yield symmetric features and can be matched wrongly, even when the rendered alignment looks plausible.

item.title: Fast Shape Retrieval Based on Differential Chain Code Descriptor and Fuzzy Contour Matching
item.description:
The problem

Matching a known shape in an image is a basic step in industrial inspection and measurement. Feature-based methods such as SIFT, SURF and ORB describe key points, but they perform poorly under heavy noise, blur or strong viewpoint change, and the many feature points make them computationally intensive. Template-based methods compare image patches directly, which is costly over large search spaces and sensitive to scale, rotation and illumination. This paper therefore matches contours, using the structural and topological information they carry.

A chain code turns a contour into a sequence of direction changes, so two similar shapes produce similar sequences and matching becomes sequence comparison. The catch is that the sequence is ordered: one noise point shifts the correspondence of the points after it, and the longer the code, the more points are misaligned and the larger the error.

How it works

The method first turns each contour into an ordered, evenly spaced point set and encodes it as differential chain codes. It then matches the local contour against the model in short segments, so that a noise point only disturbs the segment it falls in, and finally checks each candidate position geometrically.

  1. Extract, smooth and resample the contour. Run-length encoding of the binary image, a connectivity analysis and a depth-first search give the outer and inner contours, with points about 1 pixel apart. The points are smoothed with the mean of their neighbours and then sampled at a fixed distance, which reduces their number while keeping the shape.
  2. Encode the turning angles. Instead of computing an ordinary chain code first, each point and its two neighbours form two vectors, and the rotation angle between them is quantised into a differential code. The contour becomes a code sequence that does not change when the shape is translated.
  3. Match short segments. The code of the local contour is divided into short segments. Each segment slides along the longer model code, and at every position the cost is the sum of absolute code differences. Each segment produces one cost array as long as the model code.
  4. Combine the costs and pick candidates. A sliding window writes the minimum cost inside the window into its centre, which absorbs small shifts of the best position. The segment cost arrays are then combined into one total cost. The total forms valleys; positions with small cost are kept, and the centre of each valley becomes a candidate starting position.
  5. Verify with SVD. Fuzzy matching can also return look-alike or wrong positions. For each candidate, the local points are paired with the model points, a transformation is estimated by singular value decomposition (SVD), and the mean distance between the transformed pairs scores the match. The positions with the smallest mean distance are kept. An optional ICP step refines the final alignment.

Results

Lower mean distance than Halcon and Smart on all 8 test images: 0.376–0.601 for the proposed method, against 0.694–1.027 for Halcon and 0.642–0.958 for Smart (Table 1).
0.372–0.447 with ICP refinement, with standard deviations of 0.155–0.189, against 0.269–0.483 for Halcon (Table 1).

The test material is CAD drawings captured with the SmartFlash-2020 one-click measurement sensor, an instrument for large flat products with a measurement range of up to 300 × 200 mm. Each original image was rotated clockwise by 30°, 60°, 90°, 120° and 150° and matched against the original, and further experiments test matching under multi-target interference. For the quantitative comparison, Table 1 reports the mean distance and standard deviation between the matched contour and the ground truth on eight test images, for Halcon, a baseline referred to as Smart, the proposed method, and the proposed method followed by ICP.

The proposed method has the lowest mean distance of the three methods on every image; on test image 2, for example, it is 0.426, against 1.027 for Halcon and 0.715 for Smart. ICP refinement lowers the mean distance on seven images and leaves it unchanged on image 6 (0.376), with the largest reductions on images 8, 5 and 4 (0.601 → 0.372, 0.581 → 0.391 and 0.578 → 0.419). As future work, the authors plan more advanced smoothing, an improved fuzzy matching algorithm and the use of deep learning.

item.title: Identifying frequency-domain operating deflection shapes and internal damage in structures using geometric vision method
item.description:
The problem

An operating deflection shape (ODS) describes how a structure deforms at each vibration frequency while it is in service. Because it does not require prior knowledge of the excitation, it offers an automatic way to assess dynamic behaviour and to detect damage. Measuring it is the hard part. Conventional contact sensors are bulky in operation and serve a single function, and non-contact laser vibrometers sample one point at a time and need complex calibration, which is impractical when many degrees of freedom are involved. Vision methods can measure dense surface motion, but stereo-DIC reconstructs displacement in the time domain first, where noise has to be filtered out and the filtering can remove high-frequency motion as well. Earlier frequency-domain triangulation methods use one camera that sees the object from several views through relative motion, so camera poses change between views, must be re-estimated at every step, and introduce phase delays.

Internal damage adds a second difficulty. Visual crack detection only sees surface defects, while vibration-based damage identification usually needs precise excitation information or contact sensors, and recent vision-based variants still rely on pseudo-excitation or heuristic steps such as denoising and clustering.

How it works

The method uses a stereo pair of still high-speed cameras with a fixed geometry. After calibration and rectification, every observed point is described by one parameter, its disparity, which makes the map from stereo image motion to the frequency-domain ODS linear. A wavelet transform of the resulting ODS fields then exposes internal damage.

  1. RANSAC calibration. Zhang’s planar-target method runs inside a RANSAC loop: random subsets of checkerboard corners are used for calibration until the averaged re-projection error meets a threshold. Corners that lose imaging precision in some poses therefore no longer bias the focal lengths, principal points and distortion factors.
  2. Stereo and temporal matching. Only the reference stereo pair is rectified. Each point of interest is matched along the epipolar line with spatial DIC, then tracked through the original left and right image sequences with temporal DIC. Rectification is applied to the tracked point coordinates rather than to whole images, which avoids interpolation errors.
  3. Depth parameterization. In the rectified geometry a point’s depth is d = Bf/δ, with baseline B, focal length f and disparity δ, so each point has one unknown instead of three. Its image motion is encoded in a state vector ξ(t) = x₁(t)/δ(t).
  4. ODS in the frequency domain. The ODS is a linear function of the state-vector change, U(ω) = Bf · Δξ(ω), obtained with a discrete Fourier transform and no triangulation step. The ODS fields at all frequencies form the response spectrum, and each peak corresponds to a full-field ODS map.
  5. Wavelet damage identification. Each ODS field is treated as an image on the left reference grid. Damage due to stiffness loss shows up as a step in the ODS, and a Haar wavelet transform produces normalized coefficients that peak at the damage. The peak gives the location and the damage degree, a relative change in ODS amplitude that reflects the local stiffness loss.

Results

ODS amplitude at 17 Hz: 1.84 mm vs 1.86 mm from a displacement transducer, a 1.1% error, against 1.80 mm (3.2%) for stereo-DIC (Section 3.4, Fig. 7).
Mean 3D reconstruction error of the calibration target: 0.014 mm vs 0.085 mm with the standard Zhang’s method (Table 3).
Damage degree 20.8% vs a theoretical 18.9% on the plate specimen, located within 0.87 mm (Section 3.4).

The test specimen is a 1.5 mm thick, 300 mm × 50 mm plate of 304 stainless steel with a blind hole, 8.0 mm in diameter and 1.0 mm deep, on the face the cameras do not see. An exciter drove it at 17 Hz, close to its first natural frequency, while the two cameras (2560 × 1920 pixels) recorded 5000 stereo pairs at 1000 fps. RANSAC calibration lowered the re-projection error from 0.088 to 0.039 (Table 2) and the mean 3D error of an 8 × 8 test target from 0.124 mm to 0.013 mm (Table 3). On the flat specimen, the depth error ranged from −0.06 to 0.09 mm (mean 0.02 mm), against −0.17 to 0.35 mm (mean 0.09 mm) with Zhang’s calibration (Fig. 6).

At the transducer location, the vision-based spectrum captured the complete set of peaks. Even at 34.4 Hz, the smallest amplitude of 0.14 mm was estimated within 0.01 mm, while stereo-DIC missed most of the components other than the resonance. The full-field ODS maps at 17.0, 51.2, 150.6 and 248.8 Hz show the amplitude falling and the shape growing more complex as frequency rises, and singular value decomposition of these fields gives the corresponding 3D mode shapes. The wavelet damage landscape peaked at 0.208; transformed to the specimen frame, the damage lies at (24.26, 195.13) mm against the actual (25.00, 196.00) mm.

The method was also applied to a 3D-printed resin blade with curved surfaces, a 340 mm chord and two internal defects (5 mm and 3 mm in diameter, 0.8 mm and 0.6 mm deep) under a 0–300 Hz sweep excitation. Spectra at three points along the chord gave six characteristic frequencies, and the corresponding ODS maps yielded the first six mode shapes without excitation information. Both defects were found, with damage degrees of 5.1% and 3.2% and maximum positioning errors of 1.08 mm and 1.11 mm.

The authors note two limits. The two separate cameras used here are not integrated enough for long-term monitoring, and they propose a compact biprism stereo optic as a path forward. The damage algorithm recovers the location and extent of internal damage but not its shape or orientation.

item.title: Precision 3D volume measurement of transparent adhesives via spectrally optimized line laser scanning and enhanced centroid extraction
item.description:
The problem

Automated dispensing machines lay down adhesive by dots, lines and coatings in electronic packaging and precision manufacturing. Pneumatic dispensers meter the adhesive through air pressure and valve opening time, and pressure fluctuations make the discharge uneven: too much adhesive overflows, too little leaves weak bonding or poor airtightness. Measuring the volume that was actually dispensed gives the data needed to calibrate the discharge. Manual measurement with calipers is slow and inaccurate, ultrasonic methods are sensitive to material properties and the environment, and electrochemical methods struggle because most adhesives are dielectric. Optical non-contact 3D measurement works well, but mainly for opaque materials.

Transparent adhesive breaks the diffuse-reflection assumption behind structured light, photometric stereo and stereo vision. Light is reflected and refracted at more than one surface, the material has no surface texture, and the reconstruction becomes inaccurate or incomplete. Earlier laser-scanning work on transparent objects either relies on complex ray tracing, at a high computational cost, or uses a multi-stage stereo framework that remains sensitive to strong cross-reflections and needs more expensive hardware.

How it works

The system is a monocular line laser scanner: a violet laser projects a stripe onto the dispensed adhesive, a CMOS camera images it, and a mobile robotic platform moves the specimen under the sensor. Camera calibration is automatic. A calibration board on a precision lifting platform is stepped through known heights; at each height the system records a laser stripe image and, with the laser off and a fixed light on, an image of the board. Merging the two gives world coordinates for the stripe centre points, and all camera parameters are then estimated together and refined by maximum likelihood with Levenberg–Marquardt iterations. This replaces the conventional two-stage calibration (at least 15 board poses, then a separate camera-to-laser step), in which errors from the first stage propagate to the second. Each scan then passes through the following steps.

  1. Complementary spectral background optimization (CSBO). The adhesive is dispensed onto a green-yellow substrate. Green-yellow is the complementary colour of violet, so the substrate absorbs the violet laser light that passes through the adhesive and suppresses the scattering and reflections it would otherwise cause, without ray-tracing models or extra equipment.
  2. Candidate centre points. Each stripe image is mean-filtered. In every pixel row, a gradient test with direction-consistency checks finds candidate regions where the gray level rises and then falls by at least a threshold K. A gray-level centre of gravity, weighted by w(I) = I / (256 − I), gives one sub-pixel candidate centre per region.
  3. Dynamic weighted multi-factor scoring (DWMF-SS). Each candidate in a row is scored on continuity (how many neighbouring-row points lie within an offset threshold), gray-level intensity, and closeness to the point kept in the previous row, with weights 0.1, 0.8 and 0.1. Candidates darker than 10% of the brightest candidate in the row or wider than 20 pixels score zero, and the highest-scoring candidate is kept.
  4. Clean centre line and depth map. Secondary screening removes anomalous jump regions shorter than a minimum continuity length, and gaps shorter than an interpolation threshold are filled by linear interpolation. The calibration parameters turn each centre line into world coordinates, and all profiles are projected into a depth map of the adhesive surface.
  5. Volume. A datum plane is fitted by principal component analysis to platform regions of interest, and a rigid-body transformation rectifies the depth map to it. Connectivity-based segmentation (3D Otsu thresholding, run-length encoding, eight-neighbourhood connectivity) isolates the adhesive. Each pixel is treated as a prism of base Δx × Δy and height z, and the volume is V = Δx·Δy·Σz.

Results

Stripe centre RMSD of 0.0682 pixels on a calibration board, against 0.2657 for Steger, 1.0253 for the gray-level centre of gravity and 0.1518 for thinning (Table 2).
1.62% mean relative volume error on the green-yellow substrate, against 4.41% on black and 8.29–8.76% on purple, pink and blue substrates (Table 4, Fig. 22).
0.0053 s per image for centre extraction, 4.66 times faster than Steger and 3.17 times faster than thinning (Table 3).

For centre extraction, the methods were first compared on a stripe image with strong edge-diffusion noise from a metallic surface. Steger’s method picked up noise points near the stripe edges, the gray-level centre of gravity failed under the noise, and thinning extracted a skeleton through noise points, while the proposed method gave a continuous, smooth centre line that follows the stripe. Against the true centre line on a calibration board, its RMSD is 74%, 93% and 55% lower than that of Steger, gray-level centre of gravity and thinning. The weights 0.1, 0.8 and 0.1 were chosen by comparing six weight sets on the noisy image.
