The method is 1.13 times slower than the plain gray-level centre of gravity because it processes extra candidate points, which the authors consider fast enough for industrial real-time use. In their system, an FPGA implementation reaches up to 18 kHz (about 55.6 µs per frame).

For volume, similar linear beads were dispensed onto green-yellow, blue, pink, purple and black substrates. Each specimen was weighed on a precision electronic balance as ground truth, and the measured volume was converted to weight with a density of 0.0011 g/mm³. Each substrate had five replicates, each measured 20 times and averaged. The green-yellow substrate gave the lowest error, with replicate errors between 1.11% and 2.25%. On the other substrates, the depth maps show varying degrees of surface distortion caused by internal optical interference. Six more complex beads on the green-yellow substrate gave errors of 2.38%, 5.57% and 8.59% for curvilinear patterns and 2.17%, 5.56% and 5.17% for annular ones (Table 5). The larger errors come from surface data missing in the depth maps: when the bead is thick or complex, it blocks the camera’s line of sight to the regions behind it, an inherent limitation of line laser triangulation. The authors point to two scans from different viewpoints as the usual remedy, and plan to extend the system to complex backgrounds and to supplement single-scan data.

item.title: Surface Smoothing based on Discrete Orthogonal Polynomial
item.description:
The problem

Triangle meshes are a versatile way to represent 3D objects in reverse design, rapid prototyping, 3D printing and virtual simulation. Meshes obtained by 3D measurement, however, carry noise introduced during scanning and digitisation, and it has to be removed in pre-processing. The difficulty is to remove the noise while preserving geometric features such as sharp edges as much as possible.

Early smoothing methods are isotropic and cannot preserve such features: a simple, fast Laplacian smoothing, for example, also contracts the surface. Anisotropic methods do better. Many of them smooth the face normals first and then update the vertices; methods that classify features during denoising often look only at local neighbourhoods and are susceptible to noise, and sparse formulations such as L0-minimisation preserve features but lead to a non-convex, slow minimisation.

How it works

The method also smooths normals first and then moves the vertices, with two changes. A face’s normal is estimated not from a single face or its immediate neighbours but from non-local similar structures: groups of faces in a wider neighbourhood that share its orientation. These normals are then filtered by fitting them with orthogonal polynomials, whose different orders do not interfere with one another.

  1. Normal tensor of a local structure. A single noisy face normal may not be accurate enough. For each face, the faces in its r-ring vote into a normal tensor, weighted by their distance and by the angle between the normals; the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue is the representative direction of that local structure.
  2. Co-aligned local structure. Faces whose normal deviates from this direction by more than a threshold angle θth are removed, which eliminates faces with large errors from the structure. The threshold is set larger for noisier models.
  3. Non-local similar structures. The search is widened to an R-ring (R > r). Every co-aligned structure in it whose angle to the current one is within θth (40° for high noise, 20° for low noise) is added to the face’s set of non-local similar structures.
  4. Orthogonal polynomial filtering. The face normals of these structures are stacked as rows of a matrix, which is reshaped to be close to square. Discrete Legendre polynomial bases are built in the X and Y directions on [−1, 1], and the matrix is fitted with them. Where structures overlap, each face’s estimates are accumulated and divided by how often the face was used, giving its updated normal.
  5. Vertex update. Each vertex is moved according to the updated normals of the faces around it, and the mesh is updated over several iterations.

Results

Cube (noise 0.2 lₑ): MSAE 0.075 × 10⁻², against 0.135 × 10⁻² for the next-best method, UNF, together with the lowest vertex error, Ev 1.224 × 10⁻³ (Table 2).
Fandisk (noise 0.4 lₑ): lowest vertex error, Ev 5.983 × 10⁻³, against 6.976 × 10⁻³ for GNF (Table 2).
Cad (noise 0.3 lₑ): lowest normal error, MSAE 0.640 × 10⁻², against 2.529 × 10⁻² for SNF (Table 2).

The method is compared with seven others: L0-minimisation, the Bilateral, Unilateral and Guided Normal Filters (BNF, UNF, GNF), the L1-median filter, the Half-kernel Laplacian Operator (HLO) and Segmentation-Driven Feature-Preserving filtering (SNF). Synthetic test meshes are made by adding zero-mean Gaussian noise whose standard deviation σn is proportional to the mean edge length lₑ. Two errors are measured against the ground truth: Ev, a vertex-based positional error, and MSAE, the mean square angular error of the face normals. The new method has the lowest value on both measures for Cube and on one of the two for Fandisk and Cad; L0-minimisation has the lowest MSAE on Fandisk and SNF the lowest Ev on Cad. On Octaflower, SNF has the lowest errors (L1 ties it on Ev), and the paper’s close-up views show the method preserving local features.

On a raw scan of the Angel model, the method lags slightly behind SNF but denoises and preserves features better than the other methods. On the same scanned Bunny with noise at three levels, it performs well at 0.1 and 0.3 but has certain limitations at 0.5. The authors note that, like other methods, it has limited robustness against excessive noise and irregular triangulation; as future work they suggest partitioning the mesh and fitting the orthogonal polynomials separately on feature parts (corners and edges) and non-feature parts.

item.title: VeinTr: Robust end-to-end full-hand vein identification with transformer
item.description:
The problem

Hand vein identification recognises a person from the vein pattern of the hand, imaged under near-infrared light. Typical systems follow four steps: locate the hand, extract a region of interest (ROI), extract features from it, and match the result against a database of enrolled hands. Earlier work built hand-crafted geometric or statistical descriptors, which suffer under perturbations such as illumination changes and noise; more recent methods learn the features with convolutional neural networks.

Even the learned methods still work on an ROI, usually cut from the palm. That brings two drawbacks. The preprocessing is complex, and accuracy depends on how robustly the ROI is extracted, which is hard in real applications. And the crop throws information away: the vein pattern across the whole hand is unique to each person, so a representation built from only part of it is potentially inferior to one that uses the full pattern.

How it works

VeinTr skips ROI extraction and takes the full-hand image directly as input. Its identification has only two steps, feature extraction and probe-to-database matching. The feature extractor combines a convolutional local feature encoder, a lightweight transformer and an MLP-based global feature decoder, and the whole network is trained end to end as a metric-learning task.

  1. No ROI crop. Conventional pipelines locate the hand and crop a palm ROI before extracting features, so veins outside the crop are lost. VeinTr feeds in the whole hand image instead.
  2. Local features. Convolution blocks (convolution, batch normalisation, PReLU) reduce the size of the 256×256 input while extracting local features, and three residual blocks refine them into a 64×64×64 local feature map.
  3. Global aggregation with attention. The feature map is cut into 16×16 patches, which are flattened and projected to a lower dimension. Three multi-head attention layers with 8 heads relate every patch to every other one, enlarging the receptive field from local to the whole hand.
  4. One feature per hand. The global feature decoder flattens the attention output and applies a two-layer MLP with batch normalisation, giving a 512-dimensional hand vein feature. Training uses the ArcFace loss, which pulls features of the same hand together and pushes different hands apart.
  5. Probe-to-database matching. The normalised features of the enrolled hands form a database matrix D. A probe hand is assigned to the identity with the highest similarity, C = argmax(D · ‖VeinTr(p)‖).

Results

Correct recognition rate 99.85 % at 850 nm and 99.92 % at 940 nm on CASIA, the highest in the paper’s comparison with six hand-crafted and six deep-learning methods (Table 1).
Equal error rate 0.10 % and 0.09 %, against 0.51 % for the best hand-crafted method (NMRT) and 3.71 % for PVSNet (Table 1).
Trained on CASIA, 98.17 % on TPV and 97.62 % on PLUSVein without retraining (Table 2).

All methods in the comparison work on a palm or finger ROI; VeinTr is the only one that uses the full hand. On CASIA, all hand-crafted methods already exceed 90 % correct recognition and NAF is close to saturation at 99.83 % and 99.50 %, so VeinTr’s lead in recognition rate is small (0.02 and 0.42 points); in equal error rate it is 0.41 points below NMRT and 3.61 below PVSNet (Table 1). For inter-dataset tests, VeinTr is trained on one dataset and tested on all three. Models trained on CASIA or TPV stay above 90 % correct recognition on every test set. PLUSVein is much smaller (420 images of 42 volunteers), and the model trained on it generalises less well, reaching 89.76 % on CASIA and 81.43 % on TPV.

The ablation study (all models trained on CASIA) shows that both parts of the network matter. Without the attention layers, the correct recognition rate drops to 83.43 % on CASIA, 65.14 % on TPV and 55.10 % on PLUSVein; without the residual blocks, it drops to 95.12 %, 75.07 % and 83.67 % (Table 3). With three attention layers the rate saturates on CASIA and peaks on TPV and PLUSVein; a fourth and fifth layer lower it, which the authors attribute to overfitting. Three residual blocks are chosen as a trade-off between recognition rate and computational cost. As future work, the authors plan to fuse full-hand vein information with full-hand print data.

item.title: Segmentation-Driven Feature-Preserving Mesh Denoising
item.description:
The problem

Mesh denoising recovers a clean triangle mesh from one contaminated by noise, for use in tasks such as 3D modelling, computer animation and industrial design. The difficulty is to remove the noise while keeping the features that define the shape: edges, boundaries and corners.

Many denoising methods based on face normals handle features by giving small weights to anisotropic surfaces, where neighbouring faces point in clearly different directions, and large weights to isotropic surfaces, where they point the same way. Even with small weights, though, the faces on anisotropic surfaces still affect the denoising outcome. Other anisotropic methods struggle when the features are buried in severe noise, and methods built on low-rank matrices are slow. Earlier attempts to guide denoising with a segmentation either hardly preserve sharp features between regions, need the number of clusters tuned by hand, cluster an already filtered mesh, or remain unsatisfactory at high noise levels.

How it works

The method partitions the noisy mesh into regions bounded by its features and then denoises each region separately, so that a face is never filtered together with faces from another region. For meshes with high noise (σn ≥ 0.3 le, in units of the mean edge length), face orientations are so distorted, or even flipped, that direct segmentation becomes unreliable; the mesh is then first pre-filtered by a convex optimisation, segmented, and the regions are mapped back onto the original noisy mesh.

  1. Why weights are not enough. In a normal-based filter, faces across a sharp edge get small weights but still take part in the update, and they still affect the denoised result near the edge.
  2. Test every edge. For each edge shared by two faces, the cosine between their normals is compared with a global threshold Nthr (the mean cosine over all edges of the mesh), and the L2-norm of an area-based edge operator D(e), built from the four vertices of the two triangles, is compared with a user-set threshold Dthr. ‖D(e)‖2 is 0 for a flat pair of triangles and grows as the dihedral angle sharpens.
  3. Grow regions from seeds. A seed face passes its label to an edge-connected face if the normal cosine exceeds Nthr or ‖D(e)‖2 is below Dthr; newly labelled faces become seeds in turn. When growth stops, a new seed is picked at random among the unlabelled faces, until every face belongs to a region.
  4. Refine small clusters. Noise can leave small clusters behind. Clusters with fewer than 50 faces are dissolved: each of their faces takes the neighbouring label with the largest sum of normal cosines over its 2-ring neighbourhood.
  5. Denoise region by region. An existing filter, here BNF, UNF, GNF or L1, updates normals and vertices using only faces of the same region, with its own parameters unchanged. The only extra parameter is Dthr.

Results

Lowest vertex error Ev on all six synthetic test models among the compared methods, tied with plain L1 on Casting (Table 2).
Dodecahedron, σn = 0.4 le: Ev falls from 13.808 to 3.878 (×10⁻³) when the backbone is added to BNF, and from 6.832 to 2.695 with GNF (Table 2).
Icosahedron, σn = 0.4 le: with BNF, MAE drops by 62.4 % (9.859° → 3.712°) and Ev by 72.0 % (Fig. 15).

The quantitative tests add zero-mean Gaussian noise, scaled to the mean edge length, to six models with known ground truth (Cube, Casting, Double torus, Dodecahedron, Icosahedron and Cad). They measure the mean angular error of the face normals (MAE, in degrees) and the vertex-based mesh-to-mesh error Ev. The comparison covers L0, BNF, UNF, GNF, L1, HLO and TGV, and the four open-source filters BNF, UNF, GNF and L1 are also run inside the segmentation backbone with the same parameters as their original versions. Embedding the backbone lowers MAE in 23 of these 24 model–filter pairs and Ev in 22 of them. For MAE the results are competitive rather than always best: TGV has the lowest MAE on Casting and L0 on Double torus. The gains in feature preservation show most clearly on the CAD-like Cube, Dodecahedron and Icosahedron, where L0, BNF and TGV leave larger errors along the edges.

Visually, the backbone helps recover the sharp tip of the Octaflower while keeping its curved regions, the ear and eye of the Nicolo model, and the features of Fandisk under severe noise (σn = 0.4 le). On raw scans, whose noise is not Gaussian, it keeps the feathers of the Angel and the hair and lips of Wilhelm, and helps restore details on the Iron and Rabbit models. Among segmentation methods used to guide the same denoiser (K-means, VSA, SDF and the proposed one), the proposed segmentation gives the lowest overall Ev (Fig. 8). The backbone also makes UNF and GNF less sensitive to their parameters (Figs. 25–28), and the refinement step reduces pits and rough edges (Fig. 29). The authors note one limitation: on a mesh with extremely sparse and irregular triangulation, such as a gear model, the segmentation is reasonable but the denoised shape does not fully recover the original shape, especially at the edges (Fig. 30).

item.title: Reconstruction of transparent objects using phase shifting profilometry based on diffusion models
item.description:
The problem

Phase shifting profilometry (PSP) projects a set of sinusoidal fringe patterns onto an object, recovers the phase from the captured intensities and turns it into 3D shape using the system calibration. Because it relies on the correct intensity of the captured fringes, it works well for objects with diffusely reflecting surfaces. On a transparent object such as glass, the projected fringes are reflected by the front and the back surface at the same time, and some light bounces several times between the two surfaces before reaching the camera. The captured pattern is then an aliased mixture of several fringe patterns, and the phase computed from it does not describe the surface being measured.

Earlier work on transparent objects falls into reflection-based methods (for example heating the surface with a laser and imaging it with an infrared camera, which is time-consuming), refraction-based methods that trace light through the object, and deep learning methods. This paper keeps a standard PSP set-up and instead removes the unwanted light from the fringe images themselves.

How it works

The authors model each captured fringe image as a sum of the front-surface pattern, the back-surface pattern, the multiple-reflection pattern and background light. They then train a conditional diffusion model to generate only the front-surface pattern from the aliased one, and pass the generated patterns to ordinary PSP.

  1. Three light paths. Fringes reach the camera after reflection from the front surface (F), a single reflection from the back surface (B), and multiple reflections between the two surfaces (M). F and B are normally the strongest components and M the weakest.
  2. A sum to undo. Each captured fringe image is S = F + B + M + A, where A is the background light. Only F, together with the background light, can be used to reconstruct the front surface, so a network p is trained to sample an estimate F* ∼ p(S; θ).
  3. Training. The front-surface pattern x0 is captured after spraying a developer onto the object, together with the aliased pattern y of the same scene. Gaussian noise e is added to x0 in a forward diffusion process (T = 2600 steps, β rising linearly from 0.0001 to 0.002), and a U-Net with residual blocks, given the noisy pattern xt, the step t and the condition y, learns to predict the noise.
  4. Sampling. Starting from pure Gaussian noise, the trained network, conditioned on the captured aliased pattern y, estimates and removes noise one step at a time until t = 0, giving the front-surface pattern F*.
  5. Conventional PSP. The estimated patterns are processed with the 4-step PSP algorithm to obtain the wrapped phase and the 3D shape of the front surface.

Results

RMS reconstruction error 0.0420 mm for a transparent cube and 0.0423 mm for a transparent hemisphere (Table 1).
0.0437 mm for a translucent object and 0.0388 mm for a partially-transparent object (Table 1).

The set-up uses a 2048 × 1536 camera, a 1280 × 1024 DLP projector and 4-step PSP. The authors tried simulation and pasting cardboard stickers onto the surface to obtain clean front-surface fringes, but simulated images differed too much from real ones and stickers are hard to apply to non-planar objects, so the dataset was built by spraying a developer. For each object, 15,000 image pairs were used for training and 1500 for testing, with the objects placed at random positions and poses. The test objects are an acrylic transparent cube (25 mm side), a glass transparent hemisphere (20 mm radius), an acrylic translucent object and a glass partially-transparent object.

For each object, the estimated front-surface pattern is compared with the pattern captured after spraying the developer, in intensity, in wrapped phase and in the reconstructed shape. The intensities are not strictly identical, but the estimated patterns have the same characteristics, and the phase values in the object regions closely agree. The translucent object is a case where refraction-based methods do not work, because light cannot pass through it. Partially-transparent objects are hard for most existing methods because the transparent and the solid parts need different reconstruction algorithms; here, light that does not come from the front surface is simply treated as noise and removed by the diffusion model.

The authors note one limitation: because the generated patterns start from Gaussian noise, some residual noise, invisible in the images, remains and can reduce the accuracy of the phase and of the 3D reconstruction. Using more diffusion steps reduces it, but they found that this increases the computational cost of both training and sampling.

item.title: A Point Cloud Contour Extraction Method based on Plane Segmentation
item.description:
The problem

Extracting contour features from point clouds is used in industrial inspection, robot operation and related fields. Point clouds from real devices contain noise and carry no topological relationships between points, which makes contours hard to detect. Plane detection has been approached with Hough transforms, region growing and iterative RANSAC; boundary extraction with triangular meshes, breakline sorting with B-spline fitting, and the alpha shape algorithm. Alpha shapes can extract the inner and outer contour points of polygons, but for point clouds with a large data volume its time complexity is high.

Plain RANSAC has a weak spot of its own: it performs well when the point cloud has obvious noise, but points that lie close to the plane, such as those of an adjacent plane, introduce errors. The paper targets the contours of the surfaces of an object, here the contours of the chips on a circuit board.

How it works

The method has two stages. Plane segmentation fuses RANSAC with PCA to split the cloud into planar point sets. Contour extraction then turns each plane into a 2D image, finds its boundary from the image gradient, and maps the boundary points back into 3D space.

  1. RANSAC proposes planes. Three far-apart points are drawn at random and a plane is fitted through them; points within a distance threshold dth of the plane join its set. After Niterate iterations the largest set is kept as the current plane and removed from the cloud, and the search repeats until fewer than Nminnum points remain.
  2. PCA refines and cleans the planes. Each set is refitted by PCA: the plane passes through the centroid, and its normal is the eigenvector of the covariance matrix with the smallest eigenvalue. Two planes whose normals differ by less than 15° are merged if more than 90% of their points lie within dth of the other plane; plane pairs with too few points are removed. This repeats until no plane can be merged or removed.
  3. Flatten each plane into an image. A rotation matrix turns the planar point cloud parallel to the XOY plane, and a projection with focal lengths and offsets maps it into a 2D image. Pixels holding object points are set to 0, all others to 1.
  4. Find the boundary from gradients. The image is smoothed with a Gaussian filter, and the gradient magnitude and direction are computed. A preliminary edge pixel is kept as a boundary point only if its value is the largest among its neighbours along the gradient direction.
  5. Map back to 3D. The boundary pixels are transformed back through the projection and the inverse rotation, giving the contour points in 3D space.

Results

Contour of one chip in 64.614 ms, against 745.253 ms for alpha shapes, on the same 62,668-point cloud (Table 1).
919 boundary points found by the proposed method, against 514 for alpha shapes (Table 1).

The experiments extract the contours of the chips on a circuit board, running on an Intel i7-12700 CPU with 16 GB of memory. For plane segmentation, the method is compared with region growing and conventional RANSAC on the same data. On the chip shown below, region growing also takes in a neighbouring region and RANSAC a strip attached below the chip, whereas PCA-RANSAC returns the chip surface alone; the paper describes its result as the one least affected by noise.

For boundary extraction the method is compared with the alpha shape algorithm. On a single chip, alpha shapes returns a sparse, broken outline, while the proposed method returns a denser, continuous one in less time.

item.title: Gap measurement method based on projection lines and convex analysis of 3D point clouds
item.description:
The problem

The gap between the lower surface of a relay and the ground is a critical factor in relay quality: it affects the relay’s conductivity and reliability, and for a qualified relay it must be less than 0.07 mm in the working state. Common displacement sensors each have drawbacks: eddy-current sensors must be customised to the measured part and are relatively costly, inductive sensors are disturbed by temperature, humidity and electromagnetic interference, capacitive sensors need a high-voltage supply and have large nonlinear error, and photoelectric sensors cope poorly with ambient light.

Optical measurement avoids contact, but each kind has a limit. Two earlier vision methods for measuring levitation gaps, Pixel Area and SelfConvNet, trade speed against accuracy: Pixel Area is fast but less accurate, SelfConvNet more accurate but slow. 2D methods also lose depth, including in occluded areas, which limits their accuracy. 3D point clouds keep that information, but their disorder and sparsity make the measurement time-consuming. On top of this, metal surfaces are prone to defects such as pits and burrs because of the limits of machining.

How it works

The method combines two measurement models. A 2D projection-line model measures the gap from a backlit image of it; a 3D surface point-cloud model locates the support surface between the relay and the ground and measures the gap against it. In inspection, the fast 2D model runs first and the 3D model checks the relays that pass.

  1. Backlit projection image. A highly directional backlight shines through the gap; it suppresses the diffraction of the illuminating light so that the edges image clearly. The camera sees the relay’s lower edge l0 and the base edge l1 as two clear straight lines with a bright gap between them.
  2. Projection lines. After guided filtering, which smooths noise while preserving edges, vertical search lines cross the region of interest, and on each line the two points with the largest Sobel gradient mark the edges. A line-deviation index discards points that differ from both neighbours by more than a threshold, which removes the noise points caused by burrs. Least-squares lines are fitted to the remaining points, and the pixel distance d between them is converted to millimetres with D = k·d, where the coefficient k is averaged over measurements of known gaps.
  3. Point-cloud clean-up. A line-laser profiler captures the relay’s lower surface as a 3D point cloud. A point is treated as an outlier when too many of its neighbours lie farther than a distance threshold. Connected-component segmentation then splits the surface into separate regions.
  4. Convex hull and centroid. Fitting a surface to the point cloud is complex, and its efficiency and accuracy are hard to guarantee together. Instead, the method builds the convex hull of the surface points with a fast convex-hull algorithm and computes the relay’s centroid, weighting each material part by its density. An object comes to rest when the resultant force and moment on it are zero, so projecting the centroid along gravity identifies the face of the hull that forms the support surface. The gap is the vertical distance from the points of the lower surface to this plane.
  5. Two-stage inspection. The projection-line model is the coarse stage and screens every relay. Relays that pass go to the point-cloud model, the fine stage, for a second measurement.

Results

Combined 2D + 3D model: average error 0.0054 mm, maximum error 0.009 mm on gaps of 0–0.1 mm, the lowest of the five models compared (Fig. 17).
False-drop rate 0.05% at 182.4 ms per relay for the combined model on 11,931 relays, against 2% at 236.8 ms for the point-cloud model alone and 5% at 19.8 ms for the projection-line model alone (Table 2).
Average error 0.0087 mm for the point-cloud model and 0.016 mm for the projection-line model (Fig. 17).

The experiments use a 4000 × 3000 camera with a highly directional backlight for the 2D images and an OPT-LPE50 3D laser profiler for the point clouds. The models are compared with Pixel Area and SelfConvNet. For accuracy, gaps from 0 to 0.1 mm at equal steps were set on a single relay. Pixel Area had the largest errors (maximum 0.047 mm, average 0.038 mm), followed by the projection-line model (0.021 and 0.016 mm), SelfConvNet (0.02 and 0.0095 mm) and the point-cloud model (0.015 and 0.0087 mm). In the linearity test, the point-cloud model followed the true gap more closely than Pixel Area and SelfConvNet, and the combined model was the most linear.

In the factory inspection test, 11,931 relays were measured, 9,247 good and 2,684 defective. The projection-line model was both more accurate and faster than Pixel Area (6.6%, 48.5 ms), and the point-cloud model beat SelfConvNet (2.6%, 510 ms) on both counts. The combined model had the lowest false-drop rate and was faster than both the point-cloud model and SelfConvNet, meeting the requirements of real-time on-site inspection. Manual inspection of mis-detected relays showed surface defects of varying degree, particularly pits and burrs. At a pit, edge occlusion makes the projection image show the lower surface at line b rather than at the pit bottom, line a, so Pixel Area, SelfConvNet and the projection-line model, which all work from projection images, lose accuracy there. The point-cloud model measures the distance between the entire surface and the support surface, which makes it less susceptible to pits. The authors sum up the trade-off: 2D methods are simple and fast but limited by the missing dimension and more prone to errors from surface defects, while 3D methods are more accurate and reliable at the cost of longer processing time.

item.title: Generative deep-learning-embedded asynchronous structured light for three-dimensional imaging
item.description:
The problem

Structured light measures 3D shape by projecting a sequence of stripe images, called fringe patterns, onto an object and photographing them from a second viewpoint. The surface bends the stripes, and the stripe phase at each pixel encodes depth. In fringe projection profilometry (FPP), one of the most popular forms of the technique, the camera must capture each pattern while it alone is on screen. That requires synchronisation between projector and camera, usually a hardware trigger signal.

Synchronisation is a practical burden. Hardware trigger circuits are found in expensive industrial equipment, while affordable consumer devices often have no interface for them, even though the cameras in smartphones, tablets and laptops now offer high resolution and frame rates. Software synchronisation waits longer than the exposure time between patterns, which lowers the frame rate and does not always work stably. Signal wires also limit how far apart camera and projector can be and are susceptible to electromagnetic interference. If projector and camera simply run independently, though, the projector can switch patterns in the middle of an exposure, and the photo records a blend of two neighbouring patterns: an aliased fringe pattern (AFP). Computing phase directly from such images leads to reconstruction errors. Earlier work on unsynchronised structured light used simple binary (black-and-white) patterns or addressed other aspects of asynchrony; to the authors’ knowledge, asynchronous capture with the widely used sinusoidal fringes had not been studied.

How it works

The mixing itself has a simple form. Each pixel of an AFP adds up what the two patterns contributed during the exposure, and the split depends on the moment the projector switched (Eq. 5). The mixing does not move pixels; it is the same at every location, a property that suits a convolutional network. The switching moment, however, is unknown and very difficult to measure, so recovering two images from one is an ill-posed, one-to-many problem. The paper treats it as image generation: a generative network learns to produce the two clean patterns, and standard phase-shifting reconstruction then applies unchanged.

  1. Synchronised capture (the reference). Each exposure sees exactly one projected pattern, so each photo holds one clean pattern.
  2. Asynchronous capture. Projector and camera each run at their own constant speed, with the camera faster so that every pattern is captured. A pattern switch inside an exposure produces an AFP that integrates the two neighbouring patterns. The paper addresses mixes of two patterns.
  3. Separation with APSNet. APSNet (aliased fringe pattern separation network) is an encoder–decoder based on U-Net: four encoding blocks with max pooling, then a decoder that upsamples with skip connections back to full resolution. It maps one AFP to the two patterns it was mixed from. It is trained as the generator of a conditional generative adversarial network (GAN): a discriminator judges generated pattern pairs against real ones, and two further loss terms, mean-squared error and structural similarity, keep the generated patterns statistically close to the projected ones. Equal weights for the three terms gave the smoothest training (Fig. 8).
  4. Phase. From three AFPs, APSNet yields four successive patterns, each shifted by a quarter period. The well-established four-step phase-shifting algorithm computes the wrapped phase, and adding the fringe order (multiples of 2π) unwraps it into a continuous phase map.
  5. 3D shape. The continuous phase is converted into the object’s 3D shape with an established FPP reconstruction model.

The training data come from a real system: an industrial camera (2048 × 1536 pixels), a DLP projector (1280 × 1024) and a self-developed microcontroller that delays the camera by a set time Δt after the projector. With Δt = 0 the system captures ordinary, non-aliased fringes. The source patterns were five sets of 256 × 256 sinusoidal fringes with 50 to 90 periods, each in four phase shifts (0, 0.5π, π, 1.5π), captured with delays from 1 to 10 ms in 1 ms steps. This gave 1500 AFPs, each paired with its two source patterns: 1125 for training and 375 for testing.

Results

Within 0.008 mm of the synchronised reconstruction along a depth profile of a statue, with a standard deviation of 0.003 mm. Depth computed directly from the AFPs is off by −5.000 to 3.600 mm, with a standard deviation of 1.713 mm (Fig. 13).
Wrapped phase within 0.035 rad of the synchronised phase along a sampled line (Fig. 11).
Absolute error below 0.006 mm on a propeller and a 3D-printed bolt, objects with large-curvature surfaces absent from the earlier tests (standard deviations 0.002 and 0.001 mm; Fig. 16).

The test objects, including statues, a car model and a sphere, were not seen by the network during training or validation. Every comparison treats the reconstruction from synchronised patterns as the benchmark. Reconstructing directly from the AFPs loses much of the shape, while the shape from APSNet’s patterns is remarkably close to the benchmark (Fig. 12). In the paper’s summary, this improves reconstruction accuracy by three orders of magnitude over using the aliased fringes directly.

The network was trained only on sinusoidal patterns, yet it also separated aliased binary patterns projected onto a sphere, a car model and a statue, without further tuning (Fig. 14). It also handled a multi-object scene of a propeller prototype, a 3D-printed bolt and a statue, with different colours and reflective materials (Fig. 15). The method assumes that each photo mixes two patterns. If the projector runs much faster than the camera, more than two patterns fall within one exposure; the authors name this more complex aliasing as a limitation and a direction for further work.

item.title: Kinematic target surface sensing based on improved deep optical flow tracking
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) measures 3D shape with one projector and one camera. The projector casts at least three phase-shifted sinusoidal fringe patterns onto the object, the camera records how the object’s height distorts them, and the phase recovered from the set of images gives the surface. Because several images are combined, the influence of ambient light and surface reflectivity is removed, which gives PSP high accuracy and robustness. However, PSP requires the object to stay still while the fringe images are captured: if it moves between captures, the images no longer line up and the phase calculation picks up errors.

If the object’s movement is known, as a rotation matrix and translation vector, the motion can be built into the phase calculation and the error removed. The difficulty is measuring that movement from images covered in fringes. Earlier work tracked markers placed on the object, and later work used SIFT features. The periodic fringes are “noise” to SIFT and cause mismatches, so the SIFT-based methods project the fringes in one colour channel of a colour camera and filter that channel out first, which needs colour equipment with a higher cost and lower frame rate than monochrome cameras. Another method tracks the object in the fringe images directly, but it is limited to 2D translation and cannot follow a rotating object.

How it works

The method tracks the object in the fringe images themselves, with an affordable monochrome camera, and handles any 2D movement, rotation included. A modified RAFT optical-flow network estimates where every object pixel has moved, a selection step keeps only the accurate estimates, and the resulting motion is fed into the phase calculation.

  1. Motion breaks PSP. The fringes stay fixed while the object rotates and translates between captures, so each pixel sees a different part of the surface in each image. The paper models this by evaluating the reference phase at the moved coordinates in every fringe image.
  2. Correlation by NCC instead of dot product. A feature encoder maps two consecutive fringe images to feature maps at 1/8 resolution, and a context encoder processes the first image. The original RAFT compares all pairs of features by a dot product; under fringe illumination the light intensity around a feature point changes as it moves through the fringes. The improved network uses normalised cross-correlation (NCC), which normalises local lighting variations, to build the 4D correlation volume and a four-level correlation pyramid.
  3. Iterative flow updates. Starting from zero flow, a GRU-based update operator looks up the correlation pyramid and refines the flow over several iterations. The 1/8-resolution result is upsampled to full resolution, giving a displacement for every pixel.
  4. Keep only accurate points. RANSAC first removes obvious outliers. Then a rotation matrix and translation vector are fitted, each point is moved by them, and points that land more than a threshold (such as 0.5 pixel) from their tracked position are discarded. The fit and the check are repeated until every remaining point meets the threshold.
  5. Reconstruct with the motion. The final rotation matrix and translation vector describe the object motion, and the correct phase of the moving object is computed from them (Eqs. 7–11 of the paper), giving its surface.

Results

RMS error 0.082–0.098 mm across five moving objects, against the reconstruction of each object when static (Table 1).
Comparable to the SIFT-based method (0.078–0.089 mm), which relies on a colour camera to separate the fringes (Table 1).
About 12 thousand points with high-accuracy optical flow are kept to compute the motion (Section 3).

The system uses a 1280 × 720 projector and a camera of the same resolution, with 4-step PSP. For training, 2000 pairs of fringe images before and after movement were captured and split 8:1:1 into training, validation and test sets. Labels came from images without fringes taken at the same positions, where SIFT gives the rotation and translation, from which each pixel’s motion is derived. The training loss converged to 0.25 pixels after 900 epochs. Counting a point as correct when its estimated displacement is within half a pixel of the SIFT-based ground truth, the NCC-enhanced network yields more correct points on the fringe images than the original RAFT (Fig. 10).

The same trained network was applied to four further objects (Fig. 13), and each was reconstructed while moving. The RMS errors of the proposed method are slightly above those of the SIFT-based method for every object, which the authors describe as comparable, while removing the need for colour equipment. The method covers movement in a 2D plane; reconstructing objects with complex 3D movement is left to future work.

item.title: Deep learning-enabled 3D multimodal fusion of cone-beam CT and intraoral mesh scans for clinically applicable tooth-bone reconstruction
item.description:
The problem

Orthodontic treatment and implant surgery are planned on 3D models of the teeth and the bone that holds them. Two kinds of scan feed these models, and each sees only part of the picture. Cone-beam CT (CBCT) is an X-ray scan that shows whole teeth, crowns and roots, inside the jaw bone. But CBCT measurements can be up to 6.9% smaller than the real objects, depending on resolution, and CBCT often fails to capture the biting surfaces accurately because of dense enamel, dental restorations, implants and orthodontic appliances. An intraoral scanner (IOS) projects light onto the teeth and records a digital impression as a surface mesh. Its shrinkage can be as low as 0.9%, making it the most accurate of the 3D digital modalities, and it captures the bite and tooth positions well, but it shows only the crowns and gums, nothing below the gum line.

Combining the two gives what clinicians need: precise crowns on the correct roots, inside the surrounding bone. Doing this by hand is slow. Both scans must first be segmented, which is hard because anatomy varies from patient to patient. The CBCT usually shows the upper and lower jaws together, often in a bite where teeth touch, while the IOS records each jaw separately. Experienced experts need at least five hours per patient, even with interactive software and semi-automatic tools, and a fully automatic, clinically applicable solution had yet to be developed.

How it works

Deep Dental Multimodal Fusion (DDMF) is an automatic pipeline with three modules: segment the CBCT, segment the intraoral scan, then fuse the two. The fused model takes the crowns from the IOS and the roots and bone from the CBCT.

  1. Segment the CBCT. TSTNet, a network built on the Swin Transformer, labels every pixel of each 2D CBCT slice as tooth, alveolar bone or background, and 3D meshes of the teeth and bone are reconstructed from the result. Training needs labels on only about 20 of the 300–600 slices in a scan. An extra training head, tooth error calibration (TEC), corrects error-prone pixels at the tooth–bone boundary; it is removed at inference, so it adds no inference time.
  2. Segment the intraoral scan. IOSNet labels each face of the IOS mesh as gum or as one of 32 teeth, numbered in the FDI system. Two new training losses help: a centroid loss keeps the predicted centre of each tooth in place, so that two teeth are not recognised as one (or one as two), and a boundary loss sharpens tooth–tooth and tooth–gum borders. The gum is then separated, leaving numbered crowns.
  3. Split the jaws in the CBCT. A point-curvature feature, the average angle between a vertex’s surface normal and those of its neighbours, marks the boundaries where teeth meet. Removing the highest-curvature vertices separates the individual teeth; the removed vertices are merged back, and the teeth are grouped into upper and lower jaws.
  4. Register. The IOS crowns of each jaw are aligned with the matching CBCT jaw in two stages: a global registration (RANSAC on FPFH features) gives a rough initial alignment, and point-to-plane ICP at three scales refines it.
  5. Replace the crowns and fuse. CBCT crown points that lie close to the IOS crown are removed and replaced with the IOS points, and Poisson reconstruction turns the merged points into one mesh. The FDI tooth numbers come from the IOS, so the fused teeth are identified individually without instance-level annotation of the CBCT slices.

Results

Average surface distance of 0.17 mm between the fused models and expert-made ground truth, over 1,003 teeth in 50 cases (Chamfer distance 0.20 mm, Hausdorff distance 0.37 mm; Table 3).
20–25 minutes per patient, against 300–400 minutes for human experts (Table 6).
94% of CBCT meshes split correctly into upper and lower jaws, against 42% for a Gaussian-curvature method and 24% for DBSCAN, on 50 patients, 31 of them in a closed bite with tight contacts (Table 5).

The study used a large real-world dataset: 503 patients with both CBCT and intraoral scans, plus 28,559 further intraoral scans, collected from hospitals and clinics in 25 provinces of China from 2018 to 2021. The ground-truth fused models were made by a committee of human experts and had been used successfully in clinical practice. The errors were small and consistent across tooth types; the first and second molars showed slightly larger errors, mainly because they are larger. Since CBCT resolution ranged from 0.125 to 0.5 mm, an error of one to two pixels is acceptable for many clinical applications, as validated by human experts and a clinical applicability test. On 20 cases, DDMF also had lower errors than reconstruction from CBCT alone (Fig. 4C–E). The paper reports no other fusion baseline, as no systematic solution existed for this task.

Each segmentation module outperformed the compared networks. TSTNet reached a Dice coefficient of 93.99% in 5-fold cross-validation, with 50 test patients per fold, ahead of UNet, UNet++, the standard Swin Transformer and the other baselines (Table 1). IOSNet (trained on 28,000 scans) reached a mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 93.70% on lower-jaw scans and 95.70% on upper-jaw scans, 1.77 and 3.52 points above DCNet, the strongest baseline (Table 2).

The framework has been integrated into clinical software that assists orthodontic treatment planning. The authors also name its limits. The jaw splitting and registration steps may fail in 6–10% of cases, which then need manual correction, and segmentation may still be error-prone in extremely complicated cases, such as patients with metal artefacts or root canal therapy. The method has been evaluated mainly from an algorithmic perspective, and the authors call for rigorous multicentre clinical trials.

item.title: 3D reconstruction of the moving object with double-shooting based on phase shifting profilometry
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) is one of the most commonly used 3D measurement techniques, valued for its high accuracy, robustness and full-field measurement. A projector casts at least three phase-shifted sinusoidal fringe patterns onto the object, and a camera views them from another angle. The object’s height distorts the fringes, the phase of the fringes describes that distortion, and the phase plus the system parameters give the 3D shape. Because several patterns are used, traditional PSP requires the object to stay still: if it moves while the patterns are projected and captured, measurement errors appear.

Frame rate is a second limit. A projector typically shows 8-bit fringe patterns at up to 120 Hz, while a camera easily exceeds 1000 Hz, so the frame rate of the reconstructed point clouds is limited by the projector. Defocusing a projector that shows binary patterns can exceed 1000 Hz, but the amount of defocus is hard to control and quantify, and high-speed cameras and projectors raise the cost considerably. The paper asks how to reconstruct moving objects at a high frame rate with low-cost equipment.

How it works

A trigger controller is added between the camera and the projector, so the camera captures each projected fringe pattern twice and collects more fringe information about the moving object. The paper then analyses how the object’s motion changes the phase across three consecutive images, builds a fringe model that includes the motion, extracts the phase under this mixed phase shift, and reuses the captured images to obtain more reconstructed frames.

  1. Double shooting. The projector shows its N phase-shifted patterns at its normal rate, and the camera is triggered twice within each projection period. Every projected pattern therefore yields two camera images of the moving object.
  2. Mixed phase shift. Two images taken under the same pattern differ only by the phase shift caused by the object’s motion. Images taken under different patterns contain this motion-induced shift as well as the ordinary PSP phase shift. For three images I1, I2, I3, the shifts are δ1 = δ2 = 0 and δ3 = 2π/N.
  3. Fringe model with motion. An object motion tracking algorithm computes the rotation–translation matrix that describes the object’s motion. It gives the coordinate transform (fn, gn) between images, and each image is written as In = a + B cos hn + C sin hn, with hn = ϕ(fn, gn) + δn, where ϕ is the phase of the reference plane.
  4. Least-squares phase. For each pixel, a, B and C are found by minimising the squared difference between the model and the captured images. Since B = cos φ and C = −sin φ, the phase change caused by the object’s shape is φ = arctan(−C / B).
  5. Image reuse. The captured images are reused: every three adjacent images give one frame of object phase, whereas traditional PSP builds each frame from its own group of images. This raises the reconstruction frame rate of the moving object while the projector speed stays limited.

Results

Mean error on the moving object: 0.1575 mm with traditional PSP, 0.0344 mm with the proposed method (Table 1).

The experimental system consists of an industrial camera (OPT-CC1-048A-RM-G, 1800 × 1600 pixels), a projector (TJ-S50, 1280 × 720 pixels) and a motorised translation stage. The measured object is a mask. The camera runs at 20 frames/s, the stage moves at 20 mm/s, and the field of view is 70 mm × 80 mm. The mask is first reconstructed at rest with traditional PSP, and this result serves as ground truth for the error evaluation. On the moving stage, the two images taken under one projected pattern contain only the object’s motion, while images under different patterns contain both motion and fringe phase shift. The rotation–translation matrix comes from an object motion tracking algorithm, and every three adjacent images give one phase map. The proposed method reconstructs the moving mask, whereas traditional PSP applied to the moving object shows large errors.

The authors name the accuracy of the object tracking algorithm as the most important limitation: it directly sets the reconstruction accuracy, and existing tracking algorithms have difficulty describing large motions. The method can only reconstruct objects undergoing 2D translation; because of the limits of motion tracking, it cannot handle 2D rotation or 3D motion. It does not require the object to move at constant speed, but the camera must capture clear fringe images of the moving object.

item.title: Random screening-based feature aggregation for point cloud denoising
item.description:
The problem

Point clouds captured by sensing devices are contaminated by noise from the environment and the limited precision of the devices, which corrupts the geometry they describe. Traditional optimisation-based denoising needs careful parameter tuning and can struggle to remove noise and preserve features at the same time. Learning-based methods ease the tuning, but they are usually trained on data with uniform point distributions and densities, and they become less robust when the noise is severe or the point density varies.

A common way to fully exploit point position information is to fuse the features of larger patches into smaller sub-patches. That technique is typically used when the training data has a uniform point resolution, which can make the network less robust on points with varying sampling density.

How it works

The network denoises each point from its local patch. An encoder extracts point features; two random screening-based feature aggregation modules then each drop half of the points at random and fuse the global feature of the denser patch into the remaining, sparser points. Finally, point-wise weights decide how much each remaining point contributes to the displacement that moves the noisy point towards the clean surface.

  1. Build a local patch. For each noisy point, the neighbours within a ball of radius r (5 % of the bounding-box diagonal) form a patch. The patch is translated to the origin, scaled to a unit sphere, rotated into a canonical pose by PCA, and padded or downsampled to N = 500 points.
  2. Encode and screen. A graph-based encoder with Dense Blocks produces an N × C feature matrix. The network extracts a global feature from it and randomly keeps half of the point features.
  3. Fuse dense into sparse. The global feature is copied N/2 times and concatenated with the features of the screened sub-patch; an MLP turns them into an N/2 × 2C matrix. The sparser sub-patch now carries richer geometric information from the denser patch.
  4. Repeat once more. The same screening and fusion run again, leaving N/4 points with 4C channels each. In the paper’s ablation, this two-stage cascade is more effective than a single aggregation layer.
  5. Weight and move. The network regresses a weight for each of the N/4 points; a weighting loss trains points closer to the tangent plane of the patch centre to receive higher weights. The weighted features are max-pooled and decoded into a displacement vector, which is added to the noisy point. Training combines this weighting loss with a surface proximity loss.

Results

Lowest average errors on the PUNet test set: CD 2.25 and P2M 0.65 (×10⁴), against 2.40 and 0.75 for MoDNet, the next best (Table 1).
CD 2.299 and P2M 0.920 on 1,792 CAD shapes from the ABC dataset, against 2.511 and 1.104 for MoDNet and 2.719 and 1.302 for Score (Table 2).
In the ablation, the full pipeline reaches P2M 0.961, against 1.149 without feature aggregation and 1.407 without the weighting loss (Table 3).

The network is trained on PUNet’s 40 training shapes, with Gaussian noise of 0.5 % to 2 % of the bounding-sphere radius added on the fly. The PUNet test set has 20 shapes at 10,000 and 50,000 points, each with 1 %, 2 % and 3 % noise; the method has the lowest Chamfer distance (CD) and point-to-mesh distance (P2M) in most of these settings and on average. On real depth-camera scans from the Kinect Fusion dataset, whose noise differs from Gaussian noise, it has the lowest P2M on all three scans shown (Fig. 4), and it also leads on the irregularly sampled icosahedron above. The Paris-rue-Madame street scans, captured by a mobile laser scanner, have no ground truth, so that comparison is visual only (Fig. 6).

Two further checks support the design. Keeping half of the features at each screening step gives the lowest P2M, 0.961, against 1.270, 1.254 and 1.251 for ratios of 1/3, 2/3 and 3/4 (Table 4). Compared with the cascaded scale feature aggregation used in earlier work, the method performs similarly at lower noise levels but preserves geometry better under severe noise (Fig. 7). The denoised point clouds can also be turned into meshes with Poisson reconstruction, where the paper shows more accurate results on edges and complicated regions (Fig. 8).

item.title: Towards uniform point distribution in feature-preserving point cloud filtering
item.description:
The problem

Raw point clouds from scanners contain noise, so they are usually filtered before upsampling, surface reconstruction or other downstream use. A good filter should move the noisy points back onto the underlying surface, keep sharp edges and corners, and leave the points evenly spread. Existing methods tend to manage only part of this. Position-based methods such as CLOP smooth well but, since they ignore normals, tend to smear sharp features. Normal-based methods keep sharp edges better, but their filtered points are often unevenly distributed, and some that include a repulsion term still leave gaps near the edges. Deep learning methods need noisy training data with ground truth and work on local patches; they too give uneven distributions, even with a repulsion loss, and sparse or unevenly sampled inputs are hard for them.

The paper builds on the edge-aware point update of an earlier low-rank filtering method. On its own, that update moves points towards sharp edges, where they concentrate and leave gaps beside the edge. These gaps hurt downstream steps such as upsampling and surface reconstruction.

How it works

The method has two phases. It first smooths the point normals, then updates the point positions using those normals. The position update minimises the sum of two terms: an edge-aware data term that approximates the noisy surface while preserving geometric features, and a repulsion term that controls the point distribution.

  1. Noisy input. The input is a noisy point cloud with normals. If it has only positions, initial normals are estimated with principal component analysis (PCA).
  2. Normal filtering. The normals are smoothed with bilateral filtering. The quality of the filtered points depends heavily on the quality of these normals.
  3. Data term. For each point and each neighbour in its local patch, the update adjusts the angles between the vector joining the two points and their normals. This brings points onto the underlying surface and preserves sharp features, but used alone it moves points towards the edges and leaves gaps.
  4. Repulsion term. A repulsion term based on point coordinates and normals pushes neighbouring points apart perpendicular to the neighbour’s normal, with a weight that decays smoothly with distance. A parameter µ sets its strength.
  5. Iterate. Both terms are combined in one gradient-descent update per point (Eq. 6 of the paper), computed on a patch of the k nearest neighbours and repeated for t iterations. Most experiments use k = 30, µ = 0.3 and t = 5 (Table 1).

Results

Average Chamfer distance 5.80 × 10−5 on five models with synthetic noise, the lowest of the seven methods compared; the next best, RIMLS, averages 7.12 × 10−5 (Table 2).
Average mean square error 15.69 × 10−3, again the lowest average (Table 3).
0.91–28.16 s per model, faster than CLOP, TD, PCN and PF on all nine models timed (Table 5).

The method is compared with a position-based method (CLOP), two normal-based methods (GPF and RIMLS) and three deep learning methods (TotalDenoising, PointCleanNet and Pointfilter, abbreviated TD, PCN and PF). The quantitative tests use five models with synthetic Gaussian noise of 0.5 % or 1.0 % (Bunnyhi, Rockerarm, Icosahedron, Dodecahedron and Kitten). The method has the lowest Chamfer distance on four of the five models and the lowest mean square error on three. On raw scans (Nefertiti, BuddhaStele, Realscan and David) there is no ground truth, so these are compared visually; the paper reports that its method keeps details such as sharp edges, the steps of BuddhaStele and facial features better than the others. The authors attribute the low errors to the more uniform point distribution: RIMLS, for example, gives comparable visual results in some cases but larger errors in most, owing to its uneven distribution. Without the repulsion term, some points concentrate at the edges.

Further tests cover point density, noise levels from 0.5 % to 3.0 %, irregular sampling, holes and an indoor scene. The authors state two limitations: as a normal-based method it depends on the quality of the input normals, and it may give less desirable results at very high noise (1.5 % is already more challenging than 0.5 % and 1.0 %). Big holes that severely disrupt the surface are also hard to fill, and the best neighbourhood size k depends strongly on point density.

item.title: Automated reconstruction of multiple objects with individual movement based on PSP
item.description:
The problem

Phase shifting profilometry (PSP) projects several phase-shifted sinusoidal fringe patterns, normally at least three, onto an object and recovers its shape from the phase seen by a camera. Because it needs several images, the object has to stay still while they are captured. If it moves, the captured patterns no longer line up with each other and the designed phase shift between them is violated, so errors appear in the result.

The authors’ earlier work handled movement by describing it with a rotation matrix and a translation vector and building this information into the reconstruction model. It could also reconstruct several isolated objects, but only when they all had the same movement. In practice it is more common for objects to move differently, and existing methods introduce errors when multiple objects with individual movements are reconstructed.

How it works

The method gives every object its own movement description. It first finds the objects, then follows each one through the fringe sequence, computes its rotation and translation separately, and finally retrieves the phase of each object with that object’s movement.

  1. Separate fringes from the object image. The fringe patterns are projected in red and captured by a colour camera. The red component carries the fringes for phase retrieval; in the blue component the fringes are filtered out, leaving a pure object image for tracking and feature extraction.
  2. Identify the objects. In the blue image, the OTSU method separates the objects from the background. Thresholding can split an object into several parts, so a dilation step merges them again, and the contour of each object gives its bounding box.
  3. Track each object with KCF. The object inside each bounding box is used as a template, and the Kernelized Correlation Filters (KCF) tracker finds its new bounding box in the next fringe image. The new box then serves as the template for the images that follow.
  4. Estimate each object’s movement. SIFT finds feature points and their correspondences between the object before and after movement. From these points, singular value decomposition (SVD) gives a rotation matrix and translation vector for each object.
  5. Reconstruct object by object. With its own movement information, the phase of each object is retrieved from the red component by a least-squares solution of the reconstruction model that includes the movement, and the object is reconstructed. This repeats until the last object is done.

Results

RMS error 0.0773 mm with the proposed method, against 8.981 mm with traditional PSP, for two car models moving individually (Section 4, Fig. 10).

The experiment uses a colour camera (Allied Vision Manta 504C, 2452 × 2056) and a projector (Wintech DLP PRO 4500, 912 × 1140). Two car models are measured with 3-step PSP using red fringes while each one rotates and translates on the reference plane in its own way. The reference is a 6-step PSP reconstruction of the static objects. Traditional PSP shows clear movement-induced errors, which are most serious where the height changes sharply, such as at the edges of the objects; with the proposed method these errors are removed. The method can also reconstruct only selected objects and ignore the others, by choosing the objects of interest after identification.

The authors state the conditions of the method. It considers only rigid objects with two-dimensional movement. Object identification works best with a large enough intensity difference between objects and background, and because dilation enlarges the objects, they must keep some distance from each other. The fringe colour should differ strongly from the object colour, and when ambient light is weak, blue background light should be added to the projected pattern. There is no limit on movement speed, but the capture must be fast enough to give clear images.

item.title: HLO: Half-kernel Laplacian Operator for surface smoothing
item.description:
The problem

Meshes captured by scanners or other sensors always carry noise, and they have to be smoothed before shape analysis, animation or rendering. The challenge is to remove the noise while preserving features and resisting shrinkage. The uniform Laplacian, which compares each vertex with the centroid of its neighbours, smooths effectively, but being isotropic it wipes out features and shrinks the surface. The paper also analyses feature points: on a sharp edge the surface is not differentiable, so the second-order derivative that the Laplacian approximates does not exist, and applying the uniform Laplacian to such a vertex with all its neighbours does not make sense. Most feature-preserving methods instead rely on face or vertex normals, and many of them consist of multiple steps and numerous parameters that are difficult to tune, especially on complex models.

How it works

HLO keeps the simplicity of the uniform Laplacian but applies it to half windows, subsets of a vertex’s neighbours, instead of the whole neighbourhood. For every vertex it generates all of these half windows, computes a Laplacian on each, and keeps the one with the least energy. The surface is then updated iteratively with these half-kernel Laplacians.

  1. The full window fails at features. The uniform Laplacian compares a vertex v₀ with the centroid v′₀ of all its neighbours. At a vertex on a sharp edge the surface is not differentiable, so this operator is not applicable there; in practice, smoothing with it wipes out features and shrinks the mesh (Fig. 2).
  2. Split the neighbourhood into half windows. Each neighbour in turn, say A, is paired with the neighbour D that is closest to the plane through v₀, A and v′₀. The line A–D divides the neighbours into a left and a right half window.
  3. Half-window Laplacians. The uniform Laplacian is computed on each half window separately, giving vectors such as d₁ and d₂.
  4. Project onto the full-window direction. A half-window Laplacian also shifts the vertex sideways, which can flip or degenerate triangles. It is therefore projected onto the direction n of the full-window Laplacian, δ = (d·n)n. According to the paper, this ensures small Laplacian magnitudes at feature vertices and large ones elsewhere, so non-features are smoothed and features preserved.
  5. Pick the least energy and iterate. A vertex with |NV| neighbours has 2|NV| candidate half windows. HLO keeps the one with the smallest energy, the length of its Laplacian plus the vertex’s distance from its original position, and uses it to update the vertex. The only parameter is the number of iterations.

Results

One parameter, the number of iterations, against three to six for the compared normal-filtering and L0 methods (Table 1).
Fastest in every runtime test, for example 1.81 s on Armadillo (43,243 vertices) against 5.68 s for the next-fastest method, UNF, with 10 vertex iterations each (Table 3).
Lowest normal error (MSAE) in 4 of the 9 test cases, for example 9.33 × 10⁻² on Armadillo with noise σn = 0.5 lₑ against 9.59 × 10⁻² for L0 minimisation (Table 2).

HLO is compared with the uniform and cotangent Laplacians and with seven denoising methods: the bilateral mesh filter, the unilateral, bilateral and guided normal filters (UNF, BNF, GNF), L0 minimisation, cascaded normal regression (CNR) and non-local low-rank normal filtering (NLLR). Synthetic tests add zero-mean Gaussian noise whose standard deviation σn is proportional to the mean edge length lₑ; real tests use models scanned with Microsoft Kinect and the scanned Angel and Rabbit. Against the uniform Laplacian, HLO significantly alleviates shrinkage and gives much lower average vertex errors on the Julius model; the cotangent Laplacian is more geometry-aware but tends to create sharp “thorns”. Because the uniform Laplacian unfolds flipped triangles during smoothing, HLO is less sensitive to high noise than most of the compared methods. For the normal error MSAE, L0 minimisation and HLO are usually the best two. The vertex error Ev does not always agree with the visual comparison, because unfolding flipped triangles can move vertices far from their ground-truth positions. HLO was the fastest method in the runtime comparison, although its code had not been optimised or parallelised.

The authors note limitations. HLO has difficulty recovering smooth sharp edges on CAD-like models with few vertices, because it is not an edge-based operator; on real scanned CAD-like models with many vertices its results are comparable to the other methods. Like previous works it keeps the open boundaries of the input fixed, which can sometimes give undesired results.

item.title: Iteratively weighted principal component analysis and orientation consistency for normal estimation in point cloud
item.description:
Estimating accurate surface normals is a prerequisite for point cloud surface reconstruction, rendering, and geometric analysis. The standard PCA approach fits a plane to each point’s k-nearest neighbours and uses the smallest eigenvector as the normal estimate. This works well on clean, uniformly sampled point clouds but degrades in two common practical situations: in the presence of noise and outliers, which corrupt the covariance matrix, and near sharp features, where neighbours from geometrically different surface patches mix and produce averaged, incorrect normals. This paper addresses both problems. The iteratively re-weighted PCA (IWPCA) assigns lower weights to neighbours that deviate from the current normal estimate and iterates until convergence, effectively ignoring outliers and cross-feature contamination without requiring explicit outlier detection. An orientation consistency propagation step then resolves the normal sign ambiguity inherent to PCA-based estimation: starting from seed points with reliably oriented normals, consistent orientation is propagated across the cloud via a minimum spanning tree, without user interaction. Published in the International Journal of Wireless and Mobile Computing (2020), IWPCA yields more accurate angular errors than standard PCA and achieves globally consistent normal orientation on datasets with sharp features and moderate noise.

Algorithm principle

The method estimates normals by iteratively re-weighting each point’s local neighborhood so that outliers and cross-feature neighbours contribute less to the covariance estimate. A follow-up orientation propagation step resolves the normal sign ambiguity across the point cloud.

Visual material

Additional method and result figures will be added when the original assets are available.

Results and impact

The reported evaluation compares normal-estimation accuracy and orientation consistency against standard PCA-style baselines under noise, outliers, and sharp-feature contamination.

item.title: Transformation of LEGO Models
item.description:
The problem

Container stacking raises a practical question: how can containers be moved efficiently from one stack to another? This paper studies a remotely related question with LEGO: build a new LEGO model using bricks taken from an existing one. Many algorithms turn a 3D shape into a LEGO model, but constructing a LEGO model from the bricks of another model had not been explored in open literature. The task has two goals that pull against each other. Every pick-and-place (PnP) of a brick costs one move, and as many bricks of the source model as possible should end up in the target.

Physical constraints make the order of moves matter. A brick fully or partly under other bricks cannot be picked, and a brick cannot be placed where it would hang in the air. The authors also treat a top-surface brick that is completely surrounded by other bricks as not movable, because freeing it would take extra moves.

How it works

The source model is taken apart from the top down and the target is built from the bottom up, layer by layer. Two basic approaches decide how the target’s bricks are chosen, and three strategies decide where each brick comes from: straight from the source, from a buffer of bricks already removed, or from a stock with an unlimited supply. Combining them gives six algorithms, RT1–RT3 and FT1–FT3, which use seven brick shapes.

  1. Moves and constraints. Each PnP of one brick (source to buffer, source to target, buffer to target or stock to target) counts as a cost of 1. Only movable bricks, those with nothing on top and not fully surrounded, can be picked.
  2. Rigid or flexible target. In rigid transformation (RT), the target LEGO model is generated before the transformation, with large bricks used first on each layer. In flexible transformation (FT), the target is built from an interim voxelized model on the fly: a scoring rule weights each brick type by how many movable bricks of that type the source currently offers, so source bricks are used first.
  3. Strategy 1. The source is disassembled completely into the buffer, and the target is built from the buffer, with the stock filling in bricks the buffer lacks.
  4. Strategy 2. Movable source bricks go straight to the target. If none matches, the buffer is searched; if it has none either, one more layer of the source is disassembled into the buffer to uncover new bricks. The stock is used only when the source is gone.
  5. Strategy 3. No buffer. A matching movable source brick goes straight to the target; otherwise the stock supplies one.

The algorithms are compared with three metrics: the cost C, the number of PnP needed to build the target; the reuse rate R = Nr/Ns, the share of the source’s Ns bricks that end up in the target; and an overall performance P = V·R/C, where V is the number of voxels in the target model.

Results

FT3 gives the best overall performance of the six algorithms, averaged over the 56 transformations among eight models at each of seven model sizes; among the RT algorithms, RT2 is best (Fig. 7c).
Strategies 1 and 2 reach very similar reuse rates, so disassembling the whole source upfront is not worthwhile (Fig. 7b).
Ball to house with colour matching: FT3 reuses 73.0 % of the bricks at 2673 PnP, against 74.8 % at 4502 PnP for FT1 (Fig. 8).

The algorithms were tested on eight triangle mesh models converted to LEGO. In the first test, model A was transformed into each of the other seven models at about 2500 voxels per model. In the second, all eight models were transformed into each other at seven model sizes. Cost grows linearly with model size, and Strategies 1, 2 and 3 have consistently descending cost. An FT algorithm costs more than its RT counterpart because FT builds a target with more bricks. FT3 reaches a reuse rate comparable to the best RT algorithms. RT3’s reuse rate is much lower than RT1’s and RT2’s: when the target bricks are fixed in advance and there is no buffer, matching source bricks are hard to find, and on average more than half of the target bricks come from the stock. Reuse rate is not very sensitive to model size above 1700 voxels per model; smaller models reduce it.

The third test added colour: exterior bricks must match the surface colour, while interior bricks may take any colour. For the ball-to-house transformation, RT1 and RT2 reuse 61.9 % and 59.9 % of the bricks, and RT3 only 9.2 % (Fig. 9). The authors note the trade-offs: FT’s higher reuse comes with more and smaller bricks, giving weaker structures with internal sliding planes; the overall performance metric is empirical, and other scenarios may weigh cost differently. The study moves one brick at a time; reusing groups of bricks as modules is left to future work, and the results may not be directly applicable to a specific industrial application such as cargo container stacking.

item.title: Pick-and-place process sequencing for transformation of rasterized 3D structures
item.description:
The problem

Buildings can be put together from bricks or prefabricated components; in the same way, a structure can be assembled from equal-sized parts, or voxels, by pick-and-place (PnP): a machine picks up one part and places it somewhere else. The paper frames the task as transforming one rasterized structure (the source) into another (the destination). Building from a material palette is the special case in which the source is the palette. The question is which sequence of moves the machine should follow so that the total work is as small as possible.

Two things make this hard. Deciding which part goes where is an assignment problem: a brute-force search compares n! sequences, and the structures in the experiments have about 2,250 to 2,550 voxels each. The cheapest mapping is also not necessarily executable. The machine studied here is a Cartesian robot with at least three axes and a vacuum suction gripper that holds parts by their top surface, so it can only pick or place a voxel on the top surface of a structure.

How it works

The input is a closed triangle mesh for each shape. Each mesh is rasterized into voxels, with a flood fill to mark the interior. The two voxel models are then aligned, and the remaining work is motion sequencing: deciding which voxel moves where, and in which order.

  1. Align and classify. The structures are assumed to be aligned vertically already, and only horizontal translation is searched, exhaustively, to maximise their overlap. Voxels present only in the source are Movers (M), voxels present only in the destination are Voids (V), and overlapped voxels stay in place. If there are more M than V or the other way round, the extra voxels go to or come from a palette, a linear stack.
  2. Cost of one move. Moving Mi to Vj costs cij = |xj − xi| + |yj − yi| + 2zmax − zi − zj, measured in voxel sizes (Eq. 1). The part is lifted to the clearance plane zmax, moved in x and y only at that height to avoid collisions, and lowered onto Vj.
  3. Hungarian method on the full cost matrix. The costs of every M–V pair form an n × n matrix. The Hungarian method, with time complexity O(n³), returns the n pairs with the minimum total cost. This Global Optimization Strategy (GOS) gives a lower bound on the total cost, not a valid motion sequence.
  4. Top-access constraint. Lowest-cost pairs do not necessarily lead to a feasible sequence. In the paper’s eight-voxel example, one minimum-cost pairing (total cost 27) can be executed in a suitable order, but an equally cheap alternative deadlocks after two moves.
  5. Local Optimization Strategy (LOS). LOS builds the cost matrix only from the M and V on the top surfaces and applies the Hungarian method to it; when there are more M than V, it leaves some M out of that stage so that the total cost of the chosen pairs is minimum. The resulting pairs can be moved in any order. The top surfaces are then updated and the process repeats until all M have been moved. In the example, LOS needs two stages and its total cost, 27, happens to equal the lower bound.

The paper compares LOS with two further strategies that also produce valid sequences. The Greedy Selection Strategy (GSS) uses the same top-surface cost matrix but, without the Hungarian method, moves only the single lowest-cost pair at each step. The Random Selection Strategy (RSS) moves a random top-surface pair at each step.

Results

Wall → castle, 2,153 M–V pairs: LOS reaches the GOS lower bound of 91,192 in 14.9 s, while GOS itself takes 10,718 s (Table 1).
Starfish → castle, 2,016 pairs: total cost 75,891 for GOS (lower bound), 76,065 for LOS, 77,929 for GSS and 88,209 for RSS (Table 1).
LOS takes 1.8–30.4 s for every transformation in Table 1; GOS takes 6.1–10,718 s (Table 1).
